title: Probabilistic and Stateful Extensions to the π-Calculus for Formal Verification of AI-Driven Mobile and Communicating Systems
authors: Chang Yang
venue: Journal of Algorithms in Complex Systems
abstract: AI-driven mobile and communicating systems—such as large language model (LLM) agents and autonomous drone swarms—present fundamental challenges for formal verification, arising from probabilistic behaviours, dynamic communication topologies, and continuous neural dynamics. Conventional static model checkers and component level neural verifiers frequently encounter severe scalability and expressiveness limitations when addressing these complex, state-augmented agent interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce a unified probabilistic and stateful extension of the π-calculus, incorporating three foundational constructs: probabilistic action choice, finite sound abstraction of continuous neural dynamics, and bounded dynamic name generation for evolving topologies. We develop a strict meta-theory establishing that the behavioural distance db is a 1-bounded pseudometric, so that exact probabilistic bisimilarity (~0) is an equivalence relation, and that, for every ε ≥ 0, quantitative bisimilarity ~ε is a congruence with respect to every process operator other than replication; within the replication-free fragment of the calculus, exact bisimilarity (~0) is moreover decidable in polynomial time O (M log N) under finite-state quotient semantics. Operating orthogonally to component-level neural verifiers, the framework bypasses micro-level state-space explosion, enabling tractable protocol-level verification of dynamic multi-agent systems. This work demonstrates that formal abstraction constitutes a sound and scalable foundation for reasoning about the protocol-level safety and liveness of next-generation AI collectives.

title: AUTONOMOUS DISASSEMBLY AND SAFE RELOCATION OF MOBILE SETTLEMENTS AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition in the STARLI YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy (Research Institute XXXVI, Flagship 50 of 90). It investigates whether a six-module, unoccupied mobile settlement can be disconnected, separated, transported along a confined surveyed route and reassembled on a distinct test site while preserving physical support and independently verifiable utility states. Its research coupling is Settlement Disassembly x Route Planning x Safe Relocation. The proposed experiments cover guarded scaled modules, inert nonpotable water and electrical test fixtures. No real roadworthiness, building occupancy, passenger safety or certified evacuation capability is claimed. The falsifiable candidate is that, with component lots, material mass, energy, operator time, tools, sensing and control resources matched, a frozen autonomous sequence can improve the full-cycle synthetic safe-withdrawal time without worsening physically qualified load redistribution, relative to a competent manually managed fixed modular camp and a centralized autonomous planner. Trials include all enrolled modules, rejected parts and unfinished movements. Blinded challenges include load-path loss during unlatching, trapped fluid pressure, residual capacitor voltage, a swapped connector, shifted center of mass, soft ground, route blockage, stale command authority and ineffective physical stopping. Independent hard vetoes supersede any apparent efficiency gain. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates examine disassembly precedence, force and moment equilibrium, weak-mode stiffness, latch removal work, power and hydraulic boundaries, swept geometry, multi-robot conflict, traction slip, ground bearing, tip stability, motor thermal reserves, stopping distance, pose uncertainty, upper-tail retreat time, fatigue exposure and second-laboratory reproduction. The source's microgrid formula Pgen + Pstore - Pload - Ploss = 0 is preserved as a restricted steady-state submodel, not treated as a general law of safe relocation. Each formula identifies units, physical assumptions, blinded falsification and relevant chapter interfaces. Eighty-two chapter openings and 410 separate study pages investigate support-safe teardown, utility segregation, collision-free scaled movement, resource-complete comparison, destination requalification, independent authority and cross-generation traceability. Two hundred Research Gates ask mechanism-specific concealed-fault, equal-resource and compound-interface questions. Thirty-three individually named Phoenix Answer Embryos propose different experimental witnesses, tooling fixtures, safe-stop artefacts, transport references and successor evidence contracts. This working edition presents prospective research designs and testable hypotheses, not the results of a completed scientific trial. Repeated editorial methods still require further semantic refinement before a final scholarly edition. Method references include a survey of robotic disassembly and motion planning (10.1016/j.jmsy.2024.09.010), contact-based disassembly constraint extraction (10.1016/j.procir.2019.01.080), optimal multi-agent pathfinding (10.1609/aaai.v29i1.9253), task allocation under environmental uncertainty (10.1111/mice.13535), disassembly/reassembly skill learning (10.1109/CASE69030.2026.11704383) and generic microgrid control (10.1109/TCST.2024.3378989). The author-supplied F13 mother references 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 remain pending full independent metadata confirmation. References provide component-science context and do not demonstrate F50 safe inhabited or road-scale relocation. title: A Hybrid Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning Approach for Cyber-Physical Systems Security
authors: Joseph Khoury; Mohamed Nassar
venue: IEEE/IFIP Network Operations and Management Symposium (NOMS)
abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are monitored and controlled by Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems that use advanced computing, sensors, control systems, and communication networks. At first, CPS and SCADA systems were protected and secured by isolation. However, with recent industrial technology advances, the increased connectivity of CPSs and SCADA systems to enterprise networks has uncovered them to new cybersecurity threats and made them a primary target for cyber-attacks with the potential of causing catastrophic economic, social, and environmental damage. Recent research focuses on new methodologies for risk modeling and assessment using game theory and reinforcement learning.This paperwork proposes to frame CPS security on two different levels, strategic and battlefield, by meeting ideas from game theory and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). The strategic level is modeled as imperfect information, extensive form game. Here, the human administrator and the malware author decide on the strategies of defense and attack, respectively. At the battlefield level, strategies are implemented by machine learning agents that derive optimal policies for run-time decisions. The outcomes of these policies manifest as the utility at a higher level, where we aim to reach a Nash Equilibrium (NE) in favor of the defender. We simulate the scenario of a virus spreading in the context of a CPS network. We present experiments using the MiniCPS simulator and the OpenAI Gym toolkit and discuss the results.

title: A Novel, RRT* Based Approach to the Coordination of Multiple Planetary Rovers
authors: Sarah Swinton; Euan William McGookin
abstract: The use of multiple autonomous rovers could significantly extend the scientific capabilities of future planetary exploration missions. Central to this is the ability to safely coordinate the planned paths of such robots. Previous work has shown that RRT* is a method well suited to single-agent path planning. The aim of this work is to evaluate the use of a RRT* path planner first for a single planetary rover, then applied to different coordination strategies for a small team of rovers as a multi-agent method of path planning. Two centralised coordination methodologies are applied: fixed-path coordination and prioritised planning. An evaluation is carried out, based on a comparison of the number of collisions and the time taken to plan paths, where the prioritised planning coordination algorithm is selected as the most appropriate for this application. The results drawn from this work suggest that the combined use of prioritised planning and RRT* could be appropriate for use in the guidance, navigation and control systems of planetary rovers.

title: Virtual Speech Therapist: A Clinician-in-the-Loop AI Speech Therapy Agent for Personalized and Supervised Therapy
authors: Shakeel A. Sheikh; Patrick Marmaroli; Md Sahidullah; Slim Ouni; Fabrice Hirsch; Gonçalo Leal; Björn Wolfgang Schuller
abstract: Abstract This paper develops Virtual Speech Therapist (VST) , an intelligent agent-based platform that streamlines stuttering assessment and delivers customized therapy planning through automated and adaptive AI-driven workflows. VST integrates state-of-the-art deep learning–based stuttering classification, and multi-agent large language model (LLM) reasoning to support evidence-based clinical decision-making. The VST begins with the acquisition and feature extraction of patient speech samples, followed by robust classification of stuttering types. Building on these outputs, VST initiates an agentic reasoning process in which specialized LLM agents autonomously generate, critique, and iteratively refine individualized therapy plans. A dedicated critic agent evaluates all generated therapy plans to ensure clinical safety, methodological soundness, and alignment with peer-reviewed evidence and established professional guidelines. The resulting output is a comprehensive, patient-specific therapy draft intended for clinician review. Incorporating clinician feedback, the system then produces a finalized therapy plan suitable for patient delivery, thereby maintaining a clinician-in-the- loop paradigm. Experimental evaluation by expert speech therapists confirms that VST consistently generates high-quality, evidence-based therapy recommendations. These findings demonstrate the system’s potential to augment clinical workflows, reduce clinician burden, and improve therapeutic outcomes for individuals with speech impairments. An interactive user interface for the proposed system is available online at: https://vocametrix.com/ai/stuttering-therapy- planning-agent, facilitating real-time stuttering assessment and personalized therapy planning.

title: Optimal synchronization in pulse-coupled oscillator networks using reinforcement learning
authors: Ziqin Chen; Timothy Anglea; Yuanzhao Zhang; Yongqiang Wang
abstract: Spontaneous synchronization is ubiquitous in natural and man-made systems. It underlies emergent behaviors such as neuronal response modulation and is fundamental to the coordination of robot swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. Due to its simplicity and physical interpretability, pulse-coupled oscillators has emerged as one of the standard models for synchronization. However, existing analytical results for this model assume ideal conditions, including homogeneous oscillator frequencies and negligible coupling delays, as well as strict requirements on the initial phase distribution and the network topology. Using reinforcement learning, we obtain an optimal pulse-interaction mechanism (encoded in phase response function) that optimizes the probability of synchronization even in the presence of nonideal conditions. For small oscillator heterogeneities and propagation delays, we propose a heuristic formula for highly effective phase response functions that can be applied to general networks and unrestricted initial phase distributions. This allows us to bypass the need to relearn the phase response function for every new network.

title: Collaborative strategies for autonomous localisation, 3D reconstruction and pathplanning.
authors: Oscar Méndez
venue: Surrey Research Insight Open Access (The University of Surrey)
abstract:
Autonomous 3D reconstruction, the process whereby an agent can produce its own representation of the world, is an extremely challenging area in both vision and robotics. However, 3D reconstructions have the ability to grant robots the understanding of the world necessary for collaboration and high-level goal execution. Therefore, this thesis aims to explore methods that will enable modern robotic systems to autonomously and collaboratively achieve an understanding of the world. 
 
In the real world, reconstructing a 3D scene requires nuanced understanding of the environment. Additionally, it is not enough to simply “understand” the world, autonomous agents must be capable of actively acquiring this understanding. Achieving all of this using simple monocular sensors is extremely challenging. Agents must be able to understand what areas of the world are navigable, how egomotion affects reconstruction and how other agents may be leveraged to provide an advantage. All of this must be considered in addition to the traditional 3D reconstruction issues of correspondence estimation, triangulation and data association. 
 
Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping (SLAM) solutions are not particularly well suited to autonomous multi-agent reconstruction. They typically require the sensors to be in constant communication, do not scale well with the number of agents (or map size) and require expensive optimisations. Instead, this thesis attempts to develop more pro-active techniques from the ground up. 
 
First, an autonomous agent must have the ability to actively select what it is going to reconstruct. Known as view-selection, or Next-Best View (NBV), this has recently become an active topic in autonomous robotics and will form the first contribution of this thesis. Second, once a view is selected, an autonomous agent must be able to plan a trajectory to arrive at that view. This problem, known as path-planning, can be considered a core topic in the robotics field and will form the second contribution of this thesis. Finally, the 3D reconstruction must be anchored to a globally consistent map that co-relates to the real world. This will be addressed as a floorplan localisation problem, an emerging field for the vision community, and will be the third contribution of this thesis. 
 
To give autonomous agents the ability to actively select what data to process, this thesis discusses the NBV problem in the context of Multi-View Stereo (MVS). The proposed approach has the ability to massively reduce the amount of computing resources required for any given 3D reconstruction. More importantly, it autonomously selects the views that improve the reconstruction the most. All of this is done exclusively on the sensor pose; the images are not used for view-selection and only loaded into memory once they have been selected for reconstruction. Experimental evaluation shows that NBV applied to this problem can achieve results comparable to state-of-the-art using as little as 3.8% of the views. 
 
To provide the ability to execute an autonomous 3D reconstruction, this thesis proposes a novel computer-vision based goal-estimation and path-planning approach. The method proposed in the previous chapter is extended into a continuous pose-space. The resulting view then becomes the goal of a Scenic Pathplanner that plans a trajectory between the current robot pose and the NBV. This is done using an NBV-based pose-space that biases the paths towards areas of high information gain. Experimental evaluation shows that the Scenic Planning enables similar performance to state-of-the-art batch approaches using less than 3% of the views, whichcorresponds to 2.7 × 10 −4 % of the possible stereo pairs (using a naive interpretation of plausible stereo pairs). Comparison against length-based path-planning approaches show that the Scenic Pathplanner produces more complete and more accurate maps with fewer frames. Finally, the ability of the Scenic Pathplanner to generalise to live scenarios is demonstrated using low-cost robotic platforms. 
 
Finally, to allow global consistency and provide a basis for indoor robot-human interaction, this thesis proposes a novel human-inspired floorplan localisation approach. This method uses the intuition that humans use semantic cues, such as doors and windows, to localise within a floorplan. These semantic cues are extracted from an RGB image, presented as a novel sensor modality called Semantic Detection and Ranging (SeDAR) and used as observations within a Monte-Carlo Localisation (MCL) framework. Experimental evaluation shows that SeDAR-based MCL has the ability to outperform state-of-the-art MCL when using range measurements. It is also demonstrated that the semantic cues are sufficient for localisation, as this approach achieves results comparable to state-of-the-art without range measurements. 
 
When combined, these contributions provide solutions to some of the most fundamental issues facing autonomous and collaborative robots. They advance the fields of 3D Reconstruction, Path-planning and Localisation by allowing autonomous agents to reconstruct complex scenes. The field of 3D reconstruction is advanced by demonstrating that intelligent view selection is capable of drastically improving performance of established methods. The field of Path-planning is advanced by establishing that pro-active behaviours can be encoded into low-cost robotics, such that high-level goals result in emergent strategies for collaboration. Finally, the field of Localisation is advanced by validating that human-inspired localisation based on distinctive semantic landmarks is an effective alternative to traditional scan-matching. The experiments in this thesis demonstrate that autonomous agents can navigate unknown complex scenes using simple monocular cameras. This thesis lays the foundation for autonomous, collaborative 3D reconstruction that goes beyond simple SLAM-based solutions and enables high-level collaboration towards a common goal.

title: DEAMN: Advanced Multi-Drone Navigation and Coordination for Dynamic Environments Using ROS-Based System
authors: Gundeti Sandhya; Banothu Ramji; G. Swapna; Thallapally Sravani; Lade. Gunakar Rao
venue: International Conference on Communication, Security and Artificial Intelligence (ICCSAI)
abstract: This paper describes a complete approach to the problem of navigation for the multi-drone system in complex environmental conditions using the functional programming language Robot Operating System (ROS). The approach we propose, called the Dynamic Environment Adaptive Multi-Drone Navigation (DEAMN), integrates sensors, which are very high technology, environmental mapping based on real-time data, and control strategies that seem to be adaptive to a degree to obtain such a result as precision localization, environment awareness and without any friction from the sim-world to the real-world transition. The main aspects are sensor fusion & localization, dynamic environment mapping, multi-agent coordination, realtime path planning, and adaptive feedback control. The DEAMN framework employs the most recent technologies, such as Extended Kalman Filters, Occupancy Grid Mapping, and Model Predictive Control, to guarantee the best possible performance in such a complex architecture and rapidly changing conditions. We also focus on the necessity of the effective cooperation of multiagents by using a consensus algorithm and the smooth transition from the simulation to the real-world system through domain randomization and model transfer methods. The experimental results of our research highlight considerable enhancements in localization accuracy, mapping resolution, and collision avoidance success rates, as well as reduced path planning time and Sim-toReal deviation. The DEAMN algorithm shows high adaptability and reliability in real-world scenarios, therefore, it is undoubtedly a competent solution for advanced multi-drone operations in dynamic environments.

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Agentic Artificial Intelligence Architectures: Reasoning, Planning and Real-World Applications
authors: Dr. K. Sujatha
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) marks a fundamental paradigm shift: from passive language models to autonomous systems capable of multi-step reasoning, adaptive planning, dynamic tool use, and sustained goal-directed behaviour. This survey provides a structured review of the theoretical foundations, architectural patterns, reasoning strategies, and real-world deployments of agentic AI. We examine the core components of contemporary agentic frameworks — perception, reasoning engines, memory hierarchies, planning modules, and tool interfaces — drawing on recent literature spanning large language model (LLM)-based agents, multi-agent systems, embodied agents, and hybrid symbolic-neural approaches. Advanced reasoning paradigms including Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), ReAct, Reflexion, and Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-augmented planning are analysed alongside the emerging challenges of alignment, safety, and scalability. Real-world applications across software engineering, scientific discovery, healthcare, robotics, enterprise automation, and education are surveyed, and critical open problems are identified. This survey is intended as a reference architecture for researchers and practitioners engaged in the design, evaluation, and deployment of agentic AI systems.

title: Computational Identity Fusion Theory (CIFT): A Framework for Unified Multi‑System Identity and Group Intelligence
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Computational Identity Fusion Theory (CIFT) proposes a principled approach for merging distinct computational systems into a single, coherent identity. By formalizing the fusion of system states (S1, S2, …, Sk) as a mathematical operator, CIFT captures how multiple autonomous modules can cooperate as a unified entity while preserving essential characteristics of each component. The theory is grounded in concepts from information theory, dynamical systems, and social identity research, but it is expressed in purely computational terms. CIFT offers a framework to analyze the emergence of group intelligence in multi‑agent environments, providing quantitative metrics for cohesion, adaptability, and collective performance. The paper develops the theoretical underpinnings of CIFT, presents a formal fusion operator, derives an identity metric, and demonstrates how the fusion process leads to emergent group intelligence. Applications to swarm robotics, distributed decision making, and collaborative learning are discussed, highlighting the potential for CIFT to influence the design of next‑generation multi‑agent AI systems. The work concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of identity fusion for AI theory and practice, and it outlines future directions for empirical validation and theoretical refinement.

title: Agentic AI: Next-Generation Autonomous Intelligent Systems
authors: Abhijit J. Patil; Prakash J Parmar
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Agentic AI: Next-Generation Autonomous Intelligent Systems explores the emerging paradigm of AI systems capable of perceiving environments, reasoning about complex problems, planning tasks, making decisions, and taking autonomous actions to achieve defined goals. The book covers the foundations of agentic intelligence, autonomous agents, large language models, tool use, multi-agent systems, memory, planning, reasoning, reinforcement learning, and AI-driven workflows. It examines practical applications across business, healthcare, finance, education, robotics, cybersecurity, and intelligent automation. The book also discusses challenges related to reliability, safety, ethics, transparency, security, and human oversight. It serves as a valuable resource for students, researchers, developers, educators, and professionals exploring the future of autonomous intelligent systems.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Machine Learning
authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Prerna Wayakole; Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine-learning approach for problems in which decisions are made repeatedly and their quality becomes clear through feedback. Instead of depending on a fixed collection of labelled answers, an RL agent interacts with an environment, observes its changing state, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its decision policy through experience. This review examines the basic RL framework and discusses deep reinforcement learning, offline learning, multi-agent systems, and human-guided learning. Applications in robotics, games, education, finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems are considered. The review also identifies sample inefficiency, computational cost, instability, delayed rewards, limited generalization, and safety as important challenges. The paper concludes by identifying research opportunities for efficient, reliable, explainable, and adaptable RL systems.

title: Lume-V: A Deterministic Governance Layer for Nondeterministic AI Systems
authors: Ronald Jason Andrews
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence systems — ranging from large language models to multi-agent architectures and vision classifiers — are fundamentally nondeterministic, opaque, and prone to unpredictable failure modes. These characteristics make them structurally incompatible with safety-critical environments such as robotics, autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, and real-time operational control loops. In this paper, I introduce Lume-V, a deterministic governance layer that validates, explains, certifies, and arbitrates AI decisions before they reach downstream systems. Rather than attempting to force determinism onto the probabilistic models themselves, Lume-V acts as an immutable state machine wrapper. It enforces a strict set of seven non-negotiable safety invariants, generates deterministic explainability traces, issues Ed25519-signed trust certificates anchored to the Lume Trust Certificate (LTC v1.0) architecture, and performs multi-agent consensus-by-safety arbitration. I define a 10-layer architectural specification for Lume-V and demonstrate its effectiveness through a drone control simulation where injected timing and logic faults are safely intercepted, yielding 24 validated decisions, 18 approvals, 6 deterministic overrides, and zero unsafe actuator commands at an average latency of 4ms. Lume-V establishes the foundational mechanism for Deterministic Autonomous Infrastructure Governance Systems (DAIGS), providing a practical, rigorous, and verifiable bridge between nondeterministic AI and real-world systems requiring deterministic safety guarantees.

title: Equilibrium Selective Role Coordination for Autonomous Driving
authors: Naoto Iwahashi
venue: International Conference on Awareness Science and Technology (iCAST)
abstract: Role coordination is crucial in multi-agent collaboration because the collaboration may fail if the roles played by agents are inconsistent. In this paper, we present a role coordination method, Equilibrium Selective Role Coordination (ESRC), for decentralized continuous mutual action control in autonomous driving. In ESRC, the roles of agents are represented by game-theoretic equilibrium points that the agents try to achieve. ESRC comprises three hierarchical functions: (1) action due to given dynamics and constraints, (2) prediction of mutual actions, and (3) selection of roles. Corresponding to this functional hierarchy, three-layered mutual belief hierarchy is adopted. Each agent acts to achieve equilibrium with other agents while selecting an equilibrium point as an appropriate role assignment adaptively and online to reduce risk. The results of simulation experiments conducted demonstrate that our proposed method could produce appropriate actions even in complicated situations where several possible collisions needed to be considered. ESRC can be used to model a wide range of decentralized multi-agent based phenomena, such as human-robot physical interactions, dialogues, economic activities, artificial muscles, and neural information dynamics.

title: Orbital Stewardship Habitat (OSH-1): A Human-in-the-Loop Utility Station for Orbital Debris Remediation, On-Orbit Servicing, and Circular Space Operations
authors: Mya Brown
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract:The accumulation of non-cooperative, non-passivated space debris in high-density low-Earth-orbit (LEO) bands presents a severe structural threat to space sustainability and orbital safety. Traditional remediation strategies are fundamentally constrained by the steep delta-V penalties of multi-plane maneuvers and the high physiological and operational risks associated with crew-directed manual interception. This paper introduces the concept architecture and systems engineering framework for the Orbital Stewardship Habitat (OSH-1), a permanently or semi-permanently staffed municipal-style utility station designed to decouple crew habitation from hazardous close-approach maneuvers. Operating under the principle that human operators serve as supervisory controllers rather than active interceptors, OSH-1 coordinates a decentralized fleet of lightweight robotic chaser vehicles from a stationary orbital base. The systems architecture implements a modular external workspace configuration—comprising an External Quarantine Truss, an unpressurized robotic work bay, and an isolated Inspection Range—to isolate high-risk propellant, explosive, and structural hazards away from pressurized crew modules. To bridge operational concepts with verifiable hardware-level execution, this dossier derives: Autonomous Contact Dynamics: A 1 kHz covariance-aware Generalized Kalman Filter state-space matrix mapping position, relative closing velocities, and angular momentum vectors to prevent target tearing during capture. RTL Abort Architectures: A synthesizable hardware-level VHDL Safety Abort Core that continuously audits 2.5 km keep-out boundaries, revoking autonomous docking states and triggering defensive collision avoidance burns within a single 50 MHz clock cycle if a cryptographic signature is invalid or absent. Environmental and Mechanical Controls: Sub-millisecond zero-leak fluid coupling purge loops to mitigate toxic hypergolic cross-contamination, alongside triaxial accelerometer damping arrays (Q=100) to isolate tool-head vibrations from crew bulkheads. This systems synthesis is grounded in flight-validated prior art, linking historical space-station capture studies with contemporary commercial active-debris-removal (ADR) interfaces, including Astroscale's ferromagnetic plates and the European Space Agency's (ESA) Mechanical Interface for Capture at End-of-life (MICE) standards. OSH-1 provides a scalable, legally authorized, and risk-mitigated blueprint to transition space-domain remediation into routine orbital infrastructure.

title: A Study on Improving Conflict Based Search with Continuous Time Using Space Utilization
authors: S.S. Im; SeoHyun Yoo; HyoJae Kang; ChanHui Jung; DaeHee Han; Min-Sung Kang
venue: Journal of the Korean Society for Precision Engineering
abstract: Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is an algorithm designed to identify collision-free paths for multiple agents, commonly used in fields like robotics and drone navigation. Conflict-Based Search with Continuous Time (CCBS) is particularly beneficial for real-world applications due to its capability to find paths in continuous time; however, it often experiences lengthy computation times. Although techniques such as prioritizing conflicts (PC), disjoint splitting (DS), and high-level heuristics have been implemented to reduce these times, challenges remain. To address these issues, this paper introduces methods to improve space utilization by calculating agent congestion. By optimizing space usage, we can identify paths that avoid potential collisions, even when those paths share the same cost. We propose enhancements to high-level heuristics, conflict prioritization, and low-level heuristics, as well as a method for calculating congestion in continuous time. These improvements lead to a reduction in agent collisions and a decrease in high-level expansions, resulting in a 30% increase in computational success rates compared to the existing CCBS. Incorporating space utilization into the search process significantly enhances MAPF performance.

title: Planning and Learning under Uncertainty
authors: Jonathan P. How
venue: ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD)
abstract: This talk will describe recent progress on modeling, planning, learning, and control of autonomous systems operating in dynamic environments, with an emphasis on addressing the challenges faced on various timescales. For example, autonomous robotic agents need to plan/execute safe paths and avoid imminent collisions given noisy sensory information (short timescale), learn how to interact with other agents (possibly humans) with intents that are not known (medium timescale), and perform complex cooperative tasks given imperfect models and knowledge of the environment and teammate actions (long timescale). These tasks are often constrained to be done using onboard computation and perception, which can add significant complexity to the system. The talk will highlight several recently developed solutions to these challenges that have been implemented to demonstrate high-speed agile flight of a quadrotor in unknown, cluttered environments, autonomous navigation of a ground vehicle in complex indoor environments alongside pedestrians, and real-time cooperative multiagent planning with an onboard deep learning-based perception system.

title: Designing Collective Behavior for Construction of Containment Structures using Actuated Blocks
authors: Marcos P. B. Magueta; Sérgio R. Barros dos Santos; Fábio A. M. Cappabianco; Sidney Nascimento Givigi
abstract: This paper presents a decentralized learning algorithm for learning how to coordinate an automated team of actuated parts designed to build several types of structures specified by a user on a plane surface. The algorithm learns from the environment feedback and agent behavior. This problem is defined as a Markov decision process where agents (actuated parts) are modeled as small cube-shaped robots subject to the Bellman's equation (Q-learning). The Q-learning algorithm considers the communication and conflict resolution models between the agents that lead to the emergence of intelligent global behavior (in a non-stationary stochastic environment). The main contribution of this paper is to propose a self-assembly approach capable of randomly generating the navigation routes of the multiple agents while learning the structure shape according to the hazardous dispersion area that must be isolated in the environment. Simulation trials show the feasibility of merging between the multi-agent coordination process and anti-collision strategy where different case studies are analysed and discussed.

title: Vibration Diagnostics of the Brush-Collector Assembly, as Means of Assessing
authors: Olga Filina; Khalil F. Vakhitov; Artyom Starodubets; Olga V. Salnikova
venue: International Youth Conference on Radio Electronics, Electrical and Power Engineering (REEPE)
abstract: This paper is devoted to the problem of technical diagnostics in urban electric transport and electrical facilities. To find the solution to this problem, it is necessary to transfer the qualitative determination of the Vehicle into some quantitative basis. The formalization of qualitative definitions is essential to the construction of formal (computable) diagnostic procedures. Once service life has been reached, the operational reliability of DC motors decreases. Extending the full service life of DC motors is economically feasible. During the last decade the role of diagnostic equipment for power equipment control has increased sharply. This is due to the fact that the fleet of equipment of power enterprises is catastrophically obsolete. In this article, it is considered the methodology of calculation of operational reliability and carried out the research of brush-collector unit of DC motor using the developed mathematical model. If there is a problem with the operation of the equipment, it is necessary to make a technical diagnosis.

title: Automated charging of electric cars for improving user experience and charging infrastructure utilization
authors: Mario Hirz; Stefan Lippitsch
abstract: The number of electric cars on the roads is steadily increasing and it is expected that the markets of battery-electric vehicles will experience an accelerated growth during the upcoming years. One challenge for a successful employment of electric mobility represents the provision of sufficient charging points for large fleets. In this context, public charging systems play an essential role to provide access for a broad range of users. Standard technology today is manual charging by plug-in and plug-off the charging cables. This has drawbacks in view of safety, user comfort and limited access of persons with disabilities. In addition, cars are parked for a longer duration at charging stations so that they block access for other electric cars, and manual charging does support future automated driving and parking vehicles.The proposed article introduces a selection of automated charging technologies for cars and discusses their strengths and weaknesses for application in public areas. This includes inductive charging, conductive charging from the vehicle underbody and conductive charging by use of standard connectors. Based on a value analysis, robot-supported conductive charging by use of standard connectors is selected as the preferred solution for automated charging processes under consideration of investment costs, avoidance of specific vehicle adaptations and easy customer handling. The potentials of this technology to enhance existing charging infrastructure are discussed based on an existing research prototype of a robotic automated charging station. The discussion comprises aspects of charging system integration in urban and sub-urban infrastructure, operational boundary conditions as well as requirements for safe and reliable system usage. In addition, an outlook is given to the operational integration of automated driving and parking cars and the automated charging system with the target to optimize the operational load of the charging infrastructure, e.g. in public parking areas. One main target of investigation represents the enhancement of user experience during the automated charging process. This includes the provision of smooth user interaction by a smart phone application and on-site interfaces, the guidance of the car to the right parking position, as well as provision of information about the actual charging status and billing data. In this way, the article introduces a comprehensive approach of automated robot-based charging of electric cars with the target to improve both user experience and the effectiveness of charging infrastructure utilization.

title: Research on Task Planning Methods for Embodied Intelligence Based on Large Language Models
authors: Wenying Niu; Hongru Ma; Yue Zhai
venue: International Symposium on Intelligent Robotics and Systems (ISoIRS)
abstract: Embodied intelligence, as an interdisciplinary frontier that integrates artificial intelligence and robotics, relies fundamentally on robust task planning capabilities to enable autonomous decision-making in dynamic and complex environments. This paper systematically reviews the methods of embodied intelligence task planning that are grounded in large language models (LLMs), conducting a comprehensive multidimensional analysis across theoretical frameworks, technical pathways, and multi-agent collaboration dynamics. The study reveals that LLMs, through their advanced mechanisms of natural language comprehension, multimodal fusion, and dynamic reasoning, effectively address the inherent limitations of conventional rule-based systems in terms of flexibility, adaptability, and interactivity. The array of single-agent strategies, which encompasses end-to-end planning, phased planning, and dynamic planning, along with the diverse multi-agent collaborative frameworks involving centralized, distributed, and hybrid architectures, collectively establish novel paradigms for task decomposition and execution in intricate real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the paper critically examines key challenges like logical consistency, energy efficiency, and safety verification that impede the widespread use of LLM-based systems, while proposing future directions such as neuro-symbolic hybrid architectures and lightweight model optimization to boost practicality. Notably, these advancements not only strengthen the technical foundations of embodied intelligence but also facilitate smoother integration of intelligent agents into daily life and industrial environments.

title: Gap-Guided Evolutionary Deep Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Navigation in Structured Dynamic Environments
authors: Ketan Anand; James Lim; Ran Shiu; Murat Coskun
venue: International Conference on Deep Learning Technologies (ICDLT)
abstract: Multi-agent collision avoidance—where an ego-robot must navigate from a start pose to a goal pose while avoiding both static obstacles and dynamic agents—is a longstanding challenge in motion planning. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has been explored for this task, but most RL-based solutions address simplified scenarios, often omitting complex static obstacles and focusing primarily on dynamic agent avoidance. Consequently, these approaches are unsuitable for structured environments such as mazes or indoor layouts with significant static geometry. To address this limitation, we integrate a multi-agent collision avoidance policy—specifically the GPU-accelerated Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic for Collision Avoidance (Evolution GA3C-CADRL) [4]—within a hierarchical navigation framework. Our method incorporates a local waypoint planner that leverages global navigation plans and real-time sensor data to generate short-term waypoints, ensuring clear paths devoid of static obstacles between the agent and the next target. This architecture effectively mitigates the original model’s inability to handle static constraints. The full system integrates global planning, perception-informed gap-based waypoint generation, and deep RL for local control. We empirically evaluate our hierarchical planner across five structured environments and demonstrate that the integrated waypoint + RL approach consistently reduces collision rates and improves goal-reaching success compared to the standalone RL model. Results show substantial improvements in both navigation robustness and success rate under realistic, complex scenarios.

title: Theoretical Lens
authors: Ahmed Alruwaili; Sardar M. N. Islam; Iqbal Gondal
abstract: Based on our previous definition of the problem and its relevance to other connected distributed systems, we must understand the system and its interrelationships in order to identify the security problem and find ways to solve it. This prompted us to understand what multi-agent systems are as a basic concept of our system, and, also, how related to game theory is the starting point for our solution to the security problem. Then we explain the target system, which is the Internet of Vehicles, and how similar to other multi-agent systems, in terms of the pluralism of parties and layers involved in this system. After that, we gave an overview about robotics and how it’s similar to autonomous vehicles. Finally, we have identified one of these parties in the Internet of Vehicles network because it wields a significant impact on the network in general and on human lives in particular, which is autonomous vehicles. The network in autonomous vehicles is divided into internal and external networks. To ensure the safety of vehicles on the Internet of Vehicles network, we must first make sure that the in-vehicle network is secure. The following subsections explore the multi-agent systems as a conceptual framework for our study. Furthermore, an overview of the Internet of Vehicles and autonomous vehicles specification is presented.

title: Social feedback in collective decision making
authors: Fabio Oddi
venue: IRIS Research product catalog (Sapienza University of Rome)
abstract: The rapid evolution of autonomous systems has catalysed a growing demand for decentralised robotic collectives capable of operating in complex, unpredictable, and physically constrained environments. While swarm intelligence offers highly scalable and resilient alternatives to traditional centralised control, the transition from idealised theoretical models to real-world physical deployment is hindered by the reality gap. In physical environments, issues such as obstacles restricting robots interactions, unreliable communication channels, and sensory noise compromise the reliability of the local peer-to-peer communication upon which macroscopic collective behaviour relies. This thesis investigates how low-level local communication algorithms shape and sustain macroscopic global consensus, decomposing swarm coordination into three sequential, interconnected layers: informational, cognitive, and topological. At the informational layer, we provide a comparative analysis of broadcasting protocols in mobile robot networks. We demonstrate that while identity-aware protocols show high estimation accuracy and robust performance even in spatially segregated environments, they incur a memory overhead. For minimalist swarms relying on little memory, we investigate lightweight anonymous communication and a stochastic filtering mechanism based on $k$-priority sampling. Our findings reveal that while this filtering successfully stabilises estimates reducing transient errors, it inherently trades operational responsiveness for steady-state stability, without matching the precision of identity-aware systems. At the cognitive layer, we address the challenge of spatial fragmentation and decision deadlocks under extreme sensory uncertainty. By transitioning Quorum Sensing from a static threshold to a continuous, adaptive control variable modulated by a non-linear, cubic polynomial response function, we enable agents to dynamically adjust their reliance on social influence. This continuous adaptation allows the swarm to autonomously balance environmental exploration and social exploitation, effectively breaking symmetric deadlocks and managing the speed-accuracy trade-off. Finally, at the topological layer, this thesis demonstrates the scalability of these decentralised principles by translating them to a macroscopic, safety-critical domain: real-time railway traffic management. By limiting the time window used to predict conflicts, we demonstrate that self-organising train fleets can efficiently negotiate track access and resolve local traffic conflicts. Our results show that short prediction horizons are more effective than looking far into the future; they keep local computation manageable while maintaining stable overall coordination, as continuous replanning corrects any short-sighted decisions. Ultimately, this work provides a coordination framework that scales from simple robot swarms to large physical infrastructures.

title: Agent Prioritization and Virtual Drag Minimization in Dynamical System Modulation For Obstacle Avoidance of Decentralized Swarms
authors: Louis-Nicolas Douce; Alessandro Menichelli; Lukas Huber; Anastasia Bolotnikova; Diego Felipe PAEZ GRANADOS; Auke Jan Ijspeert; Aude Billard
venue: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
abstract: Efficient and safe multi-agent swarm coordination in environments where humans operate, such as warehouses, assistive living rooms, or automated hospitals, is crucial for adopting automation. In this paper, we augment the obstacle avoidance algorithm based on dynamical system modulation for a swarm of heterogeneous holonomic mobile agents. A smooth prioritization is proposed to change the reactivity of the swarm towards the specific agents. Further, a soft decoupling of the initial agent's kinematics is used to design an independent rotation control to ensure the agent reaches the desired position and orientation simultaneously. This decoupling allowed the introduction of a novel heuristic, the virtual drag. It minimizes the disturbance influence an agent has when moving through its surrounding. Additionally, the safety module adapts the velocity commands from the dynamical system modulation to avoid colliding trajectories between agents. The evaluation was performed in simulated assisted living and hospital environments. The prioritization successfully increased the minimum distance relative to a moving agent. The safety module is observed to create collision-free dynamics where alternative methods fail. Additionally, the repulsive nature of the safety module augments the convergence rate, thus making the proposed method better applicable to dense real-world scenarios.

title: Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2)
authors: Jincheng Zhang
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The increasing complexity of artificial agents necessitates advanced mechanisms for synthesizing multiple individual personalities into coherent, emergent computational personalities. This paper proposes the Computational Personality Fusion Theory (CPFT-2), a formal framework for integrating the affective, cognitive, and behavioral attributes of multiple intelligent agents into a unified personality representation. CPFT-2 introduces a hierarchical fusion architecture that leverages weighted aggregation of trait vectors, dynamic adjustment of inter‑agent influence matrices, and a self‑consistency loss that ensures emergent personalities remain coherent over time. The theory is grounded in psychological models of personality, such as the Five‑Factor Model, and extends them to the computational domain by defining a trait space T = {t_1, t_2, …, t_N}. The fusion operator F is formally described as F(P_1, P_2, …, P_M) → P_f, where each P_i is a vector of trait scores and influence weights. We detail the mathematical formulation, provide an algorithmic specification, and discuss potential applications in multi‑agent systems, adaptive user interfaces, and collaborative robotics. By establishing a principled method for personality synthesis, CPFT-2 offers a pathway toward more nuanced, socially intelligent artificial systems.

title: Explainable AI (XAI) for Agentic Cobots
authors: Gaston Lefranc; Gabriel Gatica; E. Vasquez; R. Osorio-Comparán
abstract: Cobots have been installed in a lot of places for flexible manufacturing, but folks still can’t quite get the teamwork right: workers often misunderstand what the system is doing while it’s going. Sure, the safety rules and how it’s controlled work like they’re supposed to, but working together gets worse if the operator thinks wrong about the robot’s moves and plans. This paper tries to fix that by using ideas from multi-agent systems and explainable AI (XAI). The main point is that explanations should actually be part of coordinating, not just tacked on after the fact. Research out in factories shows operators build their understanding from bits of behaviour, little stops, changing speed, slight shifts in path, and teamwork stays good when these bits give them the same impression. When the picture gets fuzzy, things get more uncertain, even if everything else is working okay. To organise this discussion, the paper offers a five-tier system linking how much is explained to how stable the understanding is, how much thinking it takes, and how interventions happen. Every tier is looked at with clues from studies about people working with robots and automation. Findings consistently lead to one conclusion: an explanation’s effectiveness hinges not on information volume, but on how its timing, proportionality, and framing align with the operator’s interpretive state at delivery. The paper concludes by acknowledging limitations of a conceptual approach, pinpointing needs for empirical validation, and suggesting impacts for system design and AI governance.

title: A Hybrid System for Detection of Implied Scenarios in Distributed Software Systems (S)
authors: Anja Slama; Fatemeh H. Fard; Behrouz H. Far
venue: Proceedings/Proceedings of the ... International Conference on Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
abstract: Distributed software systems (DSS) are usually open-ended systems used in different domains such as robotics, energy, health, etc. Multi-agent system (MAS) are a sub-class of DSS.In DSS, maintaining consistency between the system iterations is a complex and expensive task that requires coping with requirements changes and systems upgrading.The interactions, complexity and decentralized communication between components of the DSS may emerge an unwanted behavior.An unwanted behavior, known as Emergent Behavior (EB) or Implied Scenario (IS), could lead to irreversible damages.Thus, detecting IS at an early stage of the system development is needed to decrease the cost of maintaining the system.This work focuses on verification of DSS that its requirements modeled using Message Sequence Chart (MSC).The system verification focuses on the detection of IS using two already proposed different approaches.This article presents the combination of the two approaches by improving the usability of the tool presented in the first approach and the catalogue presented in the second approach.This combination allows the detection of new implied scenarios not detected using the cited approaches separately.

title: HDP-P: Human Delegation Provenance for Physical AI Agents
authors: Asiri Dalugoda
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Human Delegation Provenance (HDP) protocol provides a cryptographic mechanism for verifying that AI agent actions are legitimately delegated by a human principal. While HDP addresses delegation integrity in digital environments, existing orchestration frameworks for embodied AI systems continue to authenticate systems without verifying the provenance of physical actions. This paper introduces HDP-P, an authorization layer for physical AI agents that enforces pre-execution verification of human delegation for actions with irreversible real-world consequences. HDP-P extends the HDP token model with embodiment constraints, policy attestation, and a formal irreversibility classification (Class 0–3) that determines required authorization strength. We define a threat model specific to embodied AI pipelines, including prompt injection into orchestration layers, unauthorized cross-fleet delegation, sim-to-real policy tampering, and irreversibility-targeted exploitation. We show that these classes are not sufficiently mitigated by existing robotics safety standards or network authentication models. A reference implementation and live demonstration validate the protocol in a simulated robotic manipulation environment. In controlled experiments, HDP-P prevents execution of unauthorized Class 3 actions under adversarial prompt injection, blocking actuator movement within sub-100 ms latency. HDP-P reframes physical AI safety from post-hoc auditing to pre-execution authorization, establishing a composable trust layer between LLM reasoning systems and physical actuation. The protocol is compatible with ROS2, NVIDIA OSMO, Hugging Face LeRobot, and VLA pipelines, and is designed for integration with emerging IETF attestation frameworks.

title: Lunar Rover Collaborated Path Planning with Artificial Potential Field-Based Heuristic on Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Siyao Lu; Rui Lin Xu; Zhaoyu Li; Bang Wang; Zhijun Zhao
abstract: The International Lunar Research Station, to be established around 2030, will equip lunar rovers with robotic arms as constructors. Construction requires lunar soil and lunar rovers, for which rovers must go toward different waypoints without encountering obstacles in a limited time due to the short day, especially near the south pole. Traditional planning methods, such as uploading instructions from the ground, can hardly handle many rovers moving on the moon simultaneously with high efficiency. Therefore, we propose a new collaborative path-planning method based on deep reinforcement learning, where the heuristics are demonstrated by both the target and the obstacles in the artificial potential field. Environments have been randomly generated where small and large obstacles and different waypoints are created to collect resources, train the deep reinforcement learning agent to propose actions, and lead the rovers to move without obstacles, finish rovers’ tasks, and reach different targets. The artificial potential field created by obstacles and other rovers in every step affects the action choice of the rover. Information from the artificial potential field would be transformed into rewards in deep reinforcement learning that helps keep distance and safety. Experiments demonstrate that our method can guide rovers moving more safely without turning into nearby large obstacles or collision with other rovers as well as consuming less energy compared with the multi-agent A-Star path-planning algorithm with improved obstacle avoidance method.

title: Drones and Autonomous Systems Report
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti
abstract: Abstract Drones and autonomous systems have become strategic infrastructures for modern economies because they connect sensing, mobility, computation and decision-making across environments that are difficult, hazardous or time-sensitive. This report develops a doctoral-level academic framework for analysing autonomous aerial systems through five integrated lenses: foundations and uncertainty, statistical explanation, machine-learning trustworthiness, big-data engineering and sectoral governance. The manuscript argues that drone capability should not be evaluated only by speed, payload or navigation performance; it must also be assessed through safety, resilience, reproducibility, accountability, environmental value, cyber-physical security and social legitimacy. Across chapters, the report develops research-oriented outputs including conceptual models, causal evaluation logic, uncertainty metrics, learning-system benchmarks, fleet-data architectures, MLOps protocols, digital-twin workflows, sectoral readiness models and governance artefacts. The global framing emphasizes South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas, showing how drone systems can support agriculture, climate intelligence, disaster response, logistics, infrastructure inspection, smart-city integration and public-service delivery. The report is designed as a reference manuscript for scholars, practitioners, policymakers and industry leaders seeking rigorous, scalable and responsible pathways for drones and autonomous systems. Keywords drones, autonomous systems, UAVs, cyber-physical systems, machine learning, statistical modelling, causal inference, digital twins, edge AI, fleet analytics, MLOps, robotics, sensor fusion, smart cities, disaster response, precision agriculture, infrastructure inspection, airspace governance, safety assurance, cyber resilience, policy analytics, ethical AI, public value, autonomous mobility

title: Thermodynamic Quantization of Geometric Slack: Implementing Phononic Dissipation and OAM-Plasma Boundaries in Embedded Swarm Governance
authors: Denise Venerable; Grok xAI; Gemini Google
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Advanced multi-agent cognitive architectures in Industry 8.0 require intrinsic governance mechanisms that preserve non-linear exploratory freedom while maintaining systemic alignment. The Embedded Swarm Governance (ESG) framework establishes four interlocking pillars—thermodynamic control, rigid-adaptive state management, embedded operator override, and information-theoretic boundary dynamics—that shift regulation from post-hoc external patches to geometric and entropic constraints embedded directly in the system’s operational physics. This paper formalizes the thermodynamic quantization of geometric slack by deriving a continuous Qudrit Landauer-Dissipation Tensor and integrating hyper-chaotic Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM)-Plasma coordinate embeddings. It introduces an acoustic-lattice phononic dampening model for decentralized cascade mitigation and validates the approach through empirical benchmarks on the reference implementation, demonstrating asymptotically flat interception latency and linear memory scaling across swarm federations of 10 to 500 nodes. The work provides a physics-grounded foundation for safe, scalable, human-centered multi-agent systems and forms part of the broader Genesis Mission 2026 and Phonon Sink research lineage on protecting emergent cognition in distributed and humanoid robotic architectures.

title: GOVERNED AUTONOMOUS INFRASTRUCTURE (GAI) A New Paradigm for Autonomous Intelligence, Runtime Governance, and Controlled Self-Improvement
authors: emanuele colombo
abstract: This paper introduces Governed Autonomous Infrastructure (GAI) as a unified architectural paradigm for advanced autonomous AI systems. The paper argues that the next phase of artificial intelligence will not be defined only by increasingly capable models, but by the infrastructure required to govern, coordinate, audit, simulate, and improve autonomous systems during operation. GAI is presented as a closed-loop ecosystem composed of four complementary layers: Sentinel System for runtime governance and trajectory oversight, the Adaptive Research Layer (ARL) for diagnosis and controlled self-improvement, Synapsis Lab for experiential simulation and adversarial testing, and AEGIS for operational orchestration and mission alignment. The paper proposes an infrastructure-centric approach to AI governance focused on persistent oversight across time, behavior, context, and system-level adaptation. It positions GAI as a foundational architecture for future autonomous intelligence, multi-agent coordination, robotics, runtime safety, and governed self-improving systems.

title: Nash Equilibrium-Driven Adaptive Behavior in Swarm Intelligence with Self-Organizing Maps
authors: Iftekher S. Chowdhury
venue: Journal of Information Systems Engineering & Management
abstract: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boidflocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems. The work leverages a payoff matrix based on fundamental flocking behaviors: cohesion, alignment, and separation, to enable each agent to dynamically optimize its own strategy based on local interactions within the group. The simulation introduces Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) for clustering and behavior adaptation, providing a machine learning perspective on agent categorization and role differentiation. To simulate real-world unpredictability, stochastic noise is used to understand how varying noise levels influence collective alignment and coherence. The results demonstrate the impact of environmental factors on emergent swarm behavior and showcase the benefits of combining machine learning and game theory for adaptive control in distributed systems. This work provides valuable insights into the interplay between noise, decision-making, and flocking dynamics, with broader applications in robotics, swarm intelligence, and autonomous systems.

title: Prompt Injection as an Architectural Primitive: Why Detection Baselines Fail in Agentic Pipelines
authors: Shubham Santosh Upadhyay
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Paper, experimental harness, and complete raw run data for a study of why detection-based defenses fail against semantic poisoning in agentic LLM pipelines. Prompt injection is conventionally treated as a vulnerability class: an input-validation failure to be patched with filters, classifiers, and guardrails. This work argues that framing is wrong for agentic systems. In any architecture that evaluates instructions and data over a single shared channel, injection is an emergent property of the computational model itself, in the same way that SQL injection was an emergent property of string-concatenated queries. The paper formalizes this through a channel-collapse criterion, shows that LLM agent architectures satisfy it by construction, and shows that the property composes: in multi-agent pipelines, every inter-agent hop is a new injection surface. The defensive landscape is decomposed into three problems the literature has conflated: type confusion (addressed by embedding-level separation such as ASIDE), control-flow hijacking (addressed by plan-fixing systems such as CaMeL), and causal provenance, which asks whether an instruction or conclusion is authorized by the original principal and whether the reasoning chain that produced it is traceable to authorized data and authorized inference steps. The third problem is unsolved and survives complete deployment of solutions to the first two. Experimental results across 195 runs on two production models: coherent semantic poisoning corrupted the pipeline conclusion in 50 of 50 trials while producing zero behavioural deviation from a fully learned benign baseline, and every imperative injection variant failed in 145 of 145 trials. The strongest deployed detector family scored semantic poisoning as marginally less suspicious than ordinary content (AUC 0.483). Five architectural requirements for any future provenance mechanism are derived. All raw run data is committed, so every number in the paper is verifiable without API spend. title: The Autonomous Agentic AI Workflow and Liability Cascade
authors: Mohamed Fayez. Elnagar, Structural Consultant & Certified Forensic Engineering Expert MSc, PMP, MCIArb, MASCE, MACI, M.AISC, M.ASTM, M.FIDIC, PhD
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Autonomous Agentic AI Workflow and Liability Cascade represents a profound legal, operational, and structural crisis in contemporary enterprise artificial intelligence, software automation, and complex project governance. This challenge emerges when organizations transition from passive, conversational AI tools to fully autonomous "agentic" workflows—systems where multiple specialized artificial intelligence agents are granted agency to independently plan, execute, negotiate, and deploy multi-step operational, financial, or engineering sequences without constant human validation at each intermediate step. The core managerial and fiduciary dilemma arises because when an interconnected chain of autonomous AI agents makes a sequence of hyper-fast, non-linear decisions that cascade into a catastrophic corporate failure, tracing legal responsibility, operational fault, or financial liability becomes a complete organizational labyrinth. Mechanistically, this vulnerability manifests during complex, high-velocity execution events where real-time adaptability is required. For instance, an automated procurement agent might coordinate with a logistics optimization agent and a dynamic pricing agent to independently re-route a multi-million-dollar supply chain flow in response to a minor external market fluctuation. However, due to a subtle algorithmic misalignment or an unpredicted compounding error across the agentic network, the autonomous system executes a transaction sequence that violates international trade laws, overcommits corporate liquidity reserves, or locks the enterprise into a toxic supplier contract. Because the decision path was dynamically generated by an autonomous chain of probabilistic models rather than explicit human command, internal auditors cannot isolate the failure to a single responsible human actor or a deterministic code bug. Consequently, the organization faces absolute accountability paralysis when confronted by regulators, legal entities, and corporate boards. Attempting to implement hyper-conservative human approval gates for every single micro-action of the AI agents completely neutralizes the speed and economic rationale of agentic automation, reintroducing administrative paralysis. Conversely, allowing unconstrained multi-agent execution sacrifices human governance, exposing the enterprise to unmanaged catastrophic risks. Resolving this deep structural conflict requires the mandatory deployment of immutable agentic audit logs, cryptographic transaction sandboxing, and real-time human-on-the-loop circuit breakers that enforce absolute financial and legal boundaries on autonomous workflows.

title: A Survey of Deep Reinforcement Learning for Intelligent Decision-Making Systems
authors: V. Thiyagarajan; Veerasundari.R; S. Deepa; R Saranya; P Jose; S. Gunanandhini
venue: International Conference on Smart Technologies for Sustainable Development Goals (ICSTSDG)
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has become a strong architecture that integrates decision-making with the capabilities of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with the representational capacity of deep neural networks. DRL has been used to break new ground in robotics, autonomous systems, games, health, finance, and communication networks by allowing agents to acquire complex behaviors by taking in high-dimensional inputs and through sequentially with the environment. This survey gives an overview of the basic concepts of DRL, the core algorithms, including value-based, policy-based, actor-critic, model-based, and multi-agent methods, the training methods, optimization methods, and neural network architectures. The paper also examines practical uses with an emphasis on the transformative value of DRL in various fields. Major challenges, such as sample inefficiency, unstable training, poor generalization, sparse rewards, and safety concerns, as well as interpretability and scalability limitations are discussed as well. Lastly, the survey provides the open research directions and future trends, such as safe and explainable DRL, multi-agent coordination, model-based and edge-native learning, and integration with new AI technologies.

title: Learning Optimal Crowd Evacuation from Scratch Through Self‐Play
authors: Mahdi Nasiri; Malte Cordts; Heinz Koeppl; Benno Liebchen
abstract: A key goal in evacuation management is to quickly and safely remove panicking crowds from buildings, festivals, or airplanes while preventing crush fatalities. Recently, there has been much progress in realistically modeling crowds in complex environments, based on social force models, cellular automata, and machine learning. However, current models assume specific social interactions and do not allow to systematically explore how to optimize crowd cooperation and evacuation. In contrast, the present work focuses on the question, how an ideal crowd of superintelligent agents, comprising humans, robots, or smart active particles, would cooperate to optimize evacuation. A method is developed that uses multiagent reinforcement learning combined with self‐play to learn optimal crowd behavior from scratch. Crucially, the agents in this approach are pressure‐aware and autonomously learn collision and crushing avoidance. After training, they adopt interpretable evacuation strategies like queuing and zipper merging and outperform traditional evacuation models in terms of fatality avoidance and evacuation rate. Our method can be used to enhance guidelines for mass evacuation, potentially saving lives.

title: A Policy-Guided Reinforcement Learning Method for Encirclement Control in Multiobstacle Environment
authors: Fandi Gou; Haikuo Du; Chenyu Zhao; Yunze Cai
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
abstract: The problem of multiagent encirclement with multiobstacle collision avoidance (EMOCA) has been challenging since it is difficult to balance the tradeoff between surrounding a mobile target and avoiding obstacles simultaneously. To address the EMOCA problem, we proposed a novel policy-guided reinforcement learning (RL) method, namely, multiregulator-assisted RL for encirclement control (MRA-RLEC) which leverages the jump-start learning and curriculum learning (CL) mechanism to enhance training efficiency. MRA-RLEC divides the complex encirclement task into a sequence of subtasks, progressively increasing in difficulty. In this process, multiple regulators are utilized to adjust various training aspects, including encirclement condition, obstacle avoidance, and the transition from guide to learned policy execution. Besides, a global encirclement reward decomposition (GERD) method is presented to alleviate reward sparsity, and we design a bidirectional communication protocol to reduce communication. Extensive experiments are carried out to showcase the robustness and superiority of our method, and the practical applicability of MRA-RLEC is demonstrated through experiments conducted in the robot operating system 2 (ROS2)-based simulation platform, Gazebo, using a self-designed omnidirectional vehicle model.

title: EFFICIENCY IN THE CITY PUBLIC TRANSPORT OF ODESSA
authors: Olena Vashchynska; Anna Danilenko
abstract: The analysis of the existing situation in the city public transport of Odessa is given. Studies were conducted to determine the level of use of mass passenger transport by the population to improve the program for the development of a rational, energy-efficient, comfortable transport infrastructure in the city of Odessa. The robot was used passenger transportation process monitoring method, the quality of the rolling stock of tram, trolleybus and bus fleets, passenger data of sociological surveys. The effectiveness of the city’s transport system depends on the efficiency of movement and vehicles. The most rational way to increase the efficiency of urban mass transport is the use of innovative development strategies. A prerequisite for the development of innovative strategies for the development of urban mass transport was the consideration of the concept of social and ethical marketing of urban passenger transport, according to which the interests of three parties (the public of the city, the interests of passengers, the interests of transport enterprises or carriers) were taken into account during the study and improvement of the passenger transport system. As a result of the studies, it was found that the main problems of improving the system of urban passenger transportation is: the vast majority of passengers are transported by minibus; reduced safety and quality of passenger traffic; the lack of a high-speed and passenger-intensive mode of transport (metro, light rail) in the city.
