title: A Self-Learning Slime Mould Algorithm for Robust Multi-UAV 3D Path Planning in Complex Environments
authors: Mathias Mankoe; Fuqiang Lu; Hualing Bi; Abdul-Salam Sibidoo Mubashiru
venue: Journal of Economics Management and Trade
abstract: The autonomous navigation of UAV swarms in complex environments remains a critical bottleneck for their real-world, cost-effective deployment. This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic swarm intelligence framework, instantiated in the Self-Learning Slime Mould Algorithm (SLSMA), to address this challenge. The SLSMA empowers a UAV fleet to autonomously sense, adapt, and recover from planning failures through three core innovations: a situation-aware search strategy, a collective memory mechanism, and an adaptive recovery behavior. Rigorous evaluation on the CEC 2017 benchmark suite demonstrates that SLSMA achieves the topmost rank in the Friedman test and delivers statistically significant improvements (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p < 0.05) over eight state-of-the-art metaheuristics. In complex 3D path planning scenarios, SLSMA generates complete collision-free trajectories where competing algorithms fail, achieving a 99.5% mission success rate and reducing the total cost by up to 18.7% compared to the best-performing variant. This work holds substantial importance for the scientific community by providing a foundational shift from static optimization to adaptive, metaheuristic reasoning in swarm robotics. It establishes a new paradigm for resilient autonomy, directly addressing the critical challenge of algorithmic fragility in uncertain environments. The proposed framework offers a replicable architecture that could influence the design of future intelligent systems beyond UAV navigation. The results establish SLSMA not merely as an optimizer, but as a robust solver for resilient autonomy, paving the way for the next generation of autonomous swarms capable of persistent operation in cluttered and dynamic environments.

title: Operational Performance of a 3D Urban Aerial Network and Agent-Distributed Architecture for Freight Delivery by Drones
authors: Maria Nadia Postorino; Giuseppe M. L. Sarnè
abstract: The growing demand for fast and sustainable urban deliveries has accelerated exploration of the use of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles as viable logistics solutions for the last mile. This study investigates the integration of a distributed multi-agent system with a structured three-dimensional Urban Aerial Network (3D-UAN) for drone delivery operations. The proposed architecture models each drone as an autonomous agent operating within predefined air corridors and communication protocols. Unlike traditional approaches, which rely on simplified 2D models or centralized control systems, this research exploits a multi-layered 3D network structure combined with decentralized decision-making for improving scalability, safety, and responsiveness in complex environments. Through agent-based simulations, this study evaluates the operational performance of the proposed system under varying fleet size conditions, focusing on travel times and system scalability. Preliminary results demonstrate that the potential of this approach in supporting efficient, adaptive, resilient logistics within Urban Air Mobility frameworks depends on both the size of the fleet operating in the 3D-UAN and constraints linked to the current regulations and technological properties, such as the maximum allowed operational height. These findings contribute to ongoing efforts to define robust operational architectures and simulation methodologies for next-generation urban freight transport systems.

title: AIDR-Cloud: An Agentic AI—Driven Incident Response Framework for Cloud Failures
authors: Akshay Pratinav; Archana Kataria
abstract: Modern cloud-native systems comprise hundreds of microservices, multi-region deployments, and streaming data pipelines. This complexity has dramatically increased the frequency, impact, and opacity of operational failures. Traditional incident response, which is built around manual troubleshooting, static rules, and prewritten runbooks, struggles to meet today's latency and reliability requirements. This paper presents AIDR-Cloud, an agentic AI-driven incident detection and response framework that combines real-time telemetry, a domain-specific cloud knowledge graph, and multi-agent large language model (LLM) reasoning to autonomously diagnose [11] and remediate failures in cloud environments. AIDR-Cloud introduces a three-layer architecture: a Perception Layer that continuously ingests metrics, logs and traces; a Cognition Layer composed of specialized LLM agents that perform hypothesis generation, validation and remediation planning over a knowledge graph of cloud resources and dependencies; and an Action Layer that executes guarded remediation operations via Kubernetes and cloud-provider APIs under a safety and governance framework. We evaluate AIDR-Cloud along three complementary axes. First, in controlled fault-injection experiments on multi-region Kubernetes and Kafka workloads, we compare AIDR-Cloud against experienced human operators using standard observability and runbook tooling. Second, we analyze the cost and latency overheads of AIDR-Cloud by decomposing end-to-end response time into perception, cognition and action components, and by estimating LLM token usage, control-plane calls and infrastructure cost as a function of incident rate. Third, we report outcomes from a multi-week deployment of AIDR-Cloud on real production incidents, including changes in MTTR and escalation behavior, as well as qualitative improvements in postmortem quality and runbook evolution. Across both synthetic and real incidents, AIDR-Cloud reduces MTTR relative to the human baseline, achieves faster root-cause analysis, reduces the rate of human escalation, and selects correct remediation actions in a large fraction of cases, while adding only a small amount of reasoning latency and no unsafe actions due to strict guardrails. These results show that agentic AI can act as a statistically well-characterized and cost-conscious SRE co-pilot, significantly improving reliability and operational efficiency in complex cloud systems.

title: DualTrust: Asymmetric Bayesian Reputation and Cryptographic Gating for Autonomous AI Agents
authors: Khairan Noor Fadhlillah
abstract: Abstract The proliferation of Ambient Wearable Intelligence (AWI) ecosystems, spanning augmented reality glasses, smartwatches, and pervasive edge IoT actuators, is fundamentally transitioning human-AI interaction from explicit tactile commands to continuous, implicit background tool delegation. In these ambient environments, autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are granted operational authority to invoke external APIs, reserve financial micro-quotas, and control physical actuators. However, existing safety guardrails depend on secondary LLM-as-a-judge classifiers that introduce prohibitive runtime latencies (400–850 ms) and recurring token expenses, while static role-based access control fails against continuous behavioral drift, memory backdoors, and interleaved salami-slicing exploits. We present DualTrust, an asymmetric Bayesian reputation and cryptographic gating runtime engineered for autonomous multi-agent containment. DualTrust enforces a decoupled principal-agent architecture that strictly isolates Human Principal Accountable Credit from Bayesian Agent Operational Standing. Agent behavior is continuously modulated via an asymmetric power-law slashing engine (Δβ ∝ (sev · c^2) · v_a^1.8) with instantaneous clean-streak reset, deterministic SHA-256 64-bucket striped concurrency locks, atomically locked rollback refunds, and an O(1) RAM sliding-window RFC 6962 Merkle audit ledger with rolling epoch seals that bounds active memory consumption by committing historical roots to persistent storage. Evaluated across 176 automated invariant tests and 10,000-cycle Monte Carlo attack simulations, DualTrust makes deterministic authorization verdicts in a median latency of 47.10 µs in-memory (mean 63.16 µs, tail p99 287.10 µs) and 155.80 µs under persistent SQLite WAL disk transactions, with end-to-end Python decorator wrappers executing in median 60.70 µs (async) and 88.30 µs (sync) without external API calls. Compared against state-of-the-art LLM guardrails, DualTrust achieves over 6,600× lower latency (and over 32× to 50× lower latency than localized AST validators), by policy construction blocks Sybil defamation against collusive probation swarms, and provides tamper-evident, append-only audit durability with RFC 6962 inclusion verification, establishing a practical, foundational governance runtime for trustworthy ambient intelligence.

title: A Unified Approach for Tracking Control of MIMO Nonlinear Systems Under Unknown Control Directions and Irregular Constraints
authors: Zhuwu Shao; Yujuan Wang; Dahui Luo; Yongduan Song
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
abstract: In this work, a unified state feedback control scheme is proposed for Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) nonlinear systems subject to irregular output constraints and unknown control directions. In contrast to most existing state-of-the-art works, the constraints considered in this work can not only be asymmetric but can also appear in stages, sometimes being positive or negative. The designed controller can be applied to scenarios with or without constraints, without the need to modify or switch its structure. Moreover, it does not rely on the minimum-maximum values (MMVs) of the constraints, making it easier to implement. In addition, the issue of continuously increasing parameters in the Nussbaum function is addressed by integrating the designed bounding functions with the proposed barrier functions. This integration ensures the effectiveness of our approach regardless of the presence or absence of constraints. The effectiveness and benefits of the proposed method are verified by simulations on a planar two-link robotic manipulator.Note to Practitioners—In the majority of existing works, only scenarios with consistently present or consistently absent constraints on the system output or states are typically considered. As a result, the control methods proposed in those works are limited to either one of these scenarios, but not both. The objective of this paper is to provide a practical control solution that is suitable for both cases without the need for any switching. Moreover, in most existing works, it is necessary to possess the minimum-maximum values (MMVs) of the constraint functions. However, acquiring this information in practice entails a substantial computational burden. In this work, this restriction has been removed, thereby reducing the application conditions and increasing practicality. In addition, this work is applicable even when the control direction is unknown. This approach has been shown to be feasible through preliminary simulation experiments. In future research, the physical reality and its application to the collision avoidance control of multi-agent systems will be tried.

title: SIGMA: An Agent-Based Modeling UAV Swarm Simulator for Swarm Intelligence Algorithms
authors: Sheng Zhang; Juan Li; Chang Liu; Lei Fu; Zehao Bai; Jie Li
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
abstract: Swarm intelligence for uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) significantly improves the success rate of executing intricate tasks using “distributed platforms and aggregated effects”. However, the high experimental costs and safety risks constrain its development. This paper introduces SIGMA (Swarm Intelligence Generic simulator for Multi-UAVs), a high-fidelity distributed UAV swarm simulator for swarm intelligence algorithms. As an agent-based modeling simulator (ABMS), SIGMA has three key innovations: First, an automatic model tuning method improves aircraft dynamics fidelity. Second, a bidirectional discrete-event simulation (BiDES) architecture resolves the time alignment challenges in distributed systems. Third, a multi-agent learning toolbox ensures algorithm compatibility via an episodic training structure and a memory replay mechanism. In the verification part, the fidelity and scalability of the simulator are verified by quantitative simulations and experiments, and several successful applications demonstrate the practicality of the proposed simulator. Notice to Practitioners—The motivation for this paper stems from the need to develop a scalable and high-fidelity simulator for practical applications of swarm intelligence algorithms. Simulators developed based on game engines are widely used in swarm robotics due to their realistic 3D environments. However, as the number of nodes increases, the real-time performance and scalability of the simulators will decrease significantly. To achieve real-time simulation of large-scale swarms and improve swarm fidelity, SIGMA is proposed. It uses ABMS technology to achieve better performance and can effectively fit the learning tasks of UAV swarms.

title: Self-Adaptive Traffic Control Model With Behavior Trees and Reinforcement Learning for AGV in Industry 4.0
authors: Hao Hu; Xiaoliang Jia; Kuo Liu; Bingyang Sun
abstract: Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) are considered as an enabling technology to realize smart manufacturing in the upcoming Industrial 4.0 era. However, several challenges including efficiency, timeliness, and safety still exist in AGVs system in discrete manufacturing shopfloor. To address these challenges, a self-adaptive traffic control model combining behavior trees (BTs) and reinforcement learning (RL) is proposed to implement optimal decisions according to diverse, dynamic and complex situations in Industry 4.0 environments. A cyber-physical systems using multiagent system technology is designed in which components such as AGVs and traffic commander are defined as specific agent that cooperates autonomously with each other. Then, the behavior construction model is constructed by BTs to enumerate all the possible states in AGVs traffic control. An RL model is further developed based on the BTs. By using this approach, in this article, AGVs have the ability to adaptively choose the optimal rule-based strategy from existing optional strategies. The case study of the scenario avoiding collisions at intersections illustrates that the proposed model can enhance self-adaptive capability of AGVs traffic control and simultaneously guarantees efficiency, timeliness, and safety.

title: SpatiaVM: A Parallelized, Deterministic, and Physics-Aware Virtual Machine for Decentralized Spatial Computing and Digital Twins
authors: Mohammad Amin Moradi
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: abstractExisting blockchain Virtual Machines (VMs), such as the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) and Solana Virtual Machine (SVM), are architected strictly for 1D financial accounting and key-value state transitions. Consequently, they lack native execution support for 3D spatial geometry, deterministic physical constraints, and rotational kinematics. Applying these general-purpose financial VMs to cyber-physical systems (CPS), robotics, autonomous drone fleets, and industrial digital twins incurs cross-hardware IEEE-754 floating-point consensus splits, prohibitive gas costs, and severe $O(N)$ linear state lookup bottlenecks. To resolve these fundamental limitations, we propose SpatiaVM, a domain-specific, parallelized, and physics-aware Virtual Machine designed natively in Rust (Edition 2024). SpatiaVM introduces: (i) a bitwise deterministic Q32.32 fixed-point (Fixed64) and quaternion (QuaternionFixed) numerical engine that eliminates IEEE-754 floating-point non-determinism across heterogeneous CPU architectures; (ii) a native 3D Spatial Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) with built-in geometric collision and physical constraint enforcement opcodes; (iii) an integrated 3D Spatial Hash Grid Indexer achieving near-$O(1)$ spatial state memory lookups; (iv) dynamic volume-based spatial gas metering and ephemeral Time-To-Live (TTL) state pruning for zero-bloat database maintenance; and (v) a 3D Spatially-Partitioned Parallel Execution Scheduler that concurrently dispatches non-overlapping spatial transactions across multi-core CPUs. Empirical evaluations on a 16-core system demonstrate that SpatiaVM achieves transaction throughput exceeding 20,251 Transactions Per Second (TPS) with a $992\times$ lookup speedup over linear state scans, while logging 256-bit Merkle state root hashes and zero-knowledge execution trace commitments suitable for Layer-2 zk-STARK verification.

title: Leviathan: A Bio-Inspired, CorTexManus-Driven Marine AGI Architecture for Resilient, Long-Term Deep-Sea Exploration
authors: Khan Tahsin Abrar
abstract: Author: Khan Tahsin Abrar Affiliation: Independent Researcher, Bangladesh Email: khan.tahsin.abrar.kta@gmail.com ORC-iD: https://orcid.org/0009-0009-4631-6768 Date: August 1, 2025Important Notice:This manuscript is currently under submission at arXiv (cs.). This version is hosted temporarily on Authorea.com to ensure early public visibility and feedback. Please cite the upcoming arXiv version once it is available. AbstractThe deep ocean, constituting over 95% of the Earth’s biosphere, remains our planet’s most significant and enigmatic frontier. Exploration is severely hampered by extreme pressures, abyssal darkness, and the logistical and ethical challenges of operating in these delicate ecosystems. Current robotic platforms, predominantly tethered ROVs or task-limited AUVs, lack the cognitive autonomy, resilience, and ecological harmony required for persistent, meaningful discovery. This paper introduces Leviathan, a comprehensive architecture for a new class of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) designed for long-term, autonomous inhabitation of the deep sea. We present a complete conceptual framework and critically situate it within the state-of-the-art of cognitive robotics and marine engineering. The framework is built upon three core pillars: 1) Decentralized, Bio-inspired Cognition based on the CorTexManus (CTxM) architecture; 2) Intrinsic Resilience and Embodied Adaptation through an autonomic survival system and modular swarm intelligence; and 3) A Foundational Ethical Governance model ensuring all operations are subservient to the principle of non-disruption. We detail a system comprising a high-cognition Leviathan (LV) unit and a swarm of specialized Minnow (MW) units, proposing novel solutions for in-situ power generation, multi-modal communication, and lifecycle management. Furthermore, we outline a pragmatic AI development pipeline via the HeX-HAG framework and propose a formal validation protocol to test the architecture’s viability. This paper presents not merely a vehicle design but a rigorous blueprint for an ethically aligned, scientifically purposed artificial intelligence, complete with a research roadmap for its realization.Keywords: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), Marine Robotics, Deep-Sea Exploration, Bio-Inspired AI, CorTexManus, Modular AI Architecture, Decentralized Cognition, Ethical AI, Swarm Intelligence, Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV), AI Safety, Cognitive Robotics1. IntroductionThe deep sea is a realm of superlatives. It is the largest and least understood ecosystem on Earth, a world of crushing pressure, perpetual darkness, and chemical landscapes that defy terrestrial intuition (Jamieson, 2015). This domain holds the keys to understanding the origins of life, the limits of biology, the regulation of global climate, and vast, untapped sources of novel biomaterials. Yet, our forays into this world have been fleeting and fraught with limitations. Our primary tools, Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), are bound by physical tethers to surface ships, limiting their range and operational lifespan. Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), while untethered, typically operate on rigid, pre-programmed missions and lack the sophisticated, real-time cognitive capabilities to truly adapt, explore, and react to the unexpected discoveries that characterize the abyss (Bellingham & Rajan, 2007). These technological constraints lead to a fundamental problem: we are merely visitors to the deep, not residents. Our presence is disruptive, our observation windows are short, and our ability to conduct long-term, non-invasive studies is severely restricted. The monolithic, centralized control systems of current platforms are brittle, energy-inefficient, and ill-suited for the dynamic, unpredictable nature of the hadal zones. This paper posits that a new approach is necessary, one that shifts the paradigm from remote-controlled tools to fully autonomous, embodied, and ethically aligned artificial intelligence. We introduce Leviathan, an AGI architecture conceived from the ground up for persistent, independent operation in the deep sea. Leviathan is not a vehicle; it is an artificial organism, designed to think, survive, and explore with the efficiency and harmony of the life that has evolved there over millennia. The architectural foundation of Leviathan is the CorTexManus (CTxM) framework, a decentralized, modular cognitive model that eschews the inefficiencies of monolithic AI in favor of a distributed network of specialized processing units (Abrar, 2025a). This bio-inspired design, further elaborated in the AGI-CTxM paper, provides the blueprint for a resilient, parallel-processing mind capable of handling the immense data streams and complex decision-making required for true autonomy (Abrar, 2025b). To ensure its operations are not just effective but also responsible, Leviathan incorporates a stringent ethical governance system inspired by the principles developed for the ObsidianWingAID (OWAID) framework, ensuring that scientific discovery never comes at the cost of ecological integrity (Abrar, 2025c). This paper makes the following contributions:It presents a complete, multi-layered AGI architecture specifically designed for the challenges of deep-sea exploration.It critically situates the proposed decentralized cognitive model within the context of state-of-the-art cognitive robotic architectures.It introduces a robust ethical framework and a developmental learning path to ensure safe and responsible AI behavior in a sensitive environment.It proposes a feasible and cost-effective AI training pipeline, leveraging the HeX-HAG methodology (Abrar, 2025d).It provides a frank assessment of the system’s technological readiness and outlines a formal validation protocol and research roadmap for its future development.2. Architectural Context and Theoretical FoundationsThe Leviathan architecture is built upon a synthesis of concepts from marine robotics, bio-inspired design, and decentralized AI. This section critically evaluates these foundations and situates the proposed architecture within the current academic landscape.2.1. The State of Deep-Sea Robotics Modern deep-sea exploration relies on ROVs and AUVs. ROVs like theDeep Discoverer (NOAA) are powerful but tethered, making them extensions of human operators. AUVs like the Sentry (WHOI) offer autonomy but are limited to pre-programmed missions with minimal adaptive capability (Yoerger et al., 2007). Advanced concepts like the hybrid ROV Nereus demonstrated greater flexibility but also highlighted the extreme risks of hadal-zone operations (Kohnen, 2009). A common limitation of these systems is their centralized computational design, which creates single points of failure and is inefficient for real-time, multi-modal data fusion. Leviathan’s core design directly addresses this limitation by distributing intelligence and risk across a resilient swarm.2.2. Decentralized Cognition: The CorTexManus Paradigm The dominant trend in AI has been toward scaling monolithic models. The CorTexManus (CTxM) framework proposes a radical alternative: a distributed architecture where cognitive functions (vision, reasoning, etc.) are handled by separate, hardware-optimized TexManus Units (TxMUs) , coordinated by an AI Smart Router (AISR) (Abrar, 2025a). This emulates the brain’s functional specialization, enabling parallelism, efficiency, and resilience. The AGI-CTxM extension further introduces an autonomic survival system (Unconscious-TxMU ) and a developmental lifecycle, both of which are central to Leviathan’s design (Abrar, 2025b). While the specific formulation of CTxM is novel, its principles reflect a convergence in cognitive robotics toward decentralized and semantically aware systems. A comparative analysis reveals its unique contributions:vs. SERA (Self-Adaptive Decentralized Robotic Architecture):SERA provides a conceptual framework for fault-tolerant, self-adapting robot teams (Folino et al., 2013). Leviathan’s ”consensus arbitration” protocol for swarm reconfiguration after an LV failure is a direct implementation of SERA’s principles. CTxM can be seen as a specific, hardware-grounded instantiation of the local and global adaptation levels that SERA describes abstractly.vs. SEGO (Semantic Graph Ontology): SEGO enables robots to build ”cognitive maps” by integrating geometric perception with semantic reasoning (Zender et al., 2008). This provides a concrete methodology for the functions Leviathan’s Reasoning-TxMU must perform. To achieve true understanding, Leviathan must move beyond raw sensor data to construct such semantically rich models, identifying objects and validating observations against a knowledge base.vs. UROSA (Underwater Robot Self-Organizing Autonomy): UROSA proposes a distributed network of LLM-based AI agents for AUVs (Schiano et al., 2024). This highlights a key design trade-off: CTxM’s hardware specialization promises maximum efficiency for known tasks, while a UROSA-like system may offer greater flexibility and more nuanced, emergent reasoning from generalist LLMs. Leviathan’s hybrid approach, using specialized TxMUs that can still leverage LLM principles for reasoning, aims to capture the best of both worlds.The primary innovation of CorTexManus is its explicit, bio-inspired mapping of cognitive functions to specialized hardware, providing a clear implementation blueprint tailored for the unique constraints of an embodied, energy-scarce environment.3. The Leviathan Architecture: A System-Level Deep DiveLeviathan is conceived as a multi-component, distributed intelligence. Its architecture is layered, separating high-level cognition from autonomic survival and specialized swarm operations.3.1. The Leviathan (LV) Unit: The Central Cognitive Hub The LV unit is the heart of the system, a high-endurance AUV housing the primary AGI. Its design is predicated on the CorTexManus principle of decentralized specialization. It is coordinated by the AI Smart Router (AISR) , the system’s neural switchboard, which routes data to the appropriate TxMU.TexManus Units (TxMUs) of the LV Unit:Sonar & Acoustics TxMU (SA-TxMU): DSP-based unit for active/passive sonar, performing bathymetric mapping and acoustic signature analysis.Vision & Photonics TxMU (VP-TxMU): Power-efficient GPU for processing high-sensitivity camera feeds, specializing in the analysis of bioluminescence.Navigation & Kinematics TxMU (NK-TxMU): NPU-based ”cerebellum” fusing DVL, IMU, and pressure data for precise GPS-denied navigation via advanced SLAM algorithms.Environmental & Chemical TxMU (EC-TxMU): Interfaces with a lab-on-a-chip sensor suite for real-time chemical analysis of the water column.Reasoning & Mission-Planning TxMU (RMP-TxMU): TPU-based ”frontal lobe” for executive function, world-modeling, strategic planning, and ethical compliance verification.Communications TxMU (C-TxMU): Manages the multi-modal communication suite, switching between acoustic and optical channels.3.2. The Unconscious-TxMU (U-TxMU): The Autonomic Survival Core True resilience requires separating survival from cognition. The U-TxMU is a physically and electronically isolated, high-reliability module with ultimate authority over the AGI’s physical state. Its functions include Homeostasis Regulation (pressure, power, and thermals) and Fault Detection & ”Pain” Signaling . If a critical failure is detected, it sends a non-overridable ”pain” signal to the AISR, forcing the cognitive layer to address the physical crisis immediately.3.3. Minnow (MW) Units: The Specialized Swarm The MW units are the physical embodiment of the LV unit’s distributed cognition, functioning as Non-Autonomic Robotic-CTxM Vessels (NARCxVs) . They are small, agile, and task-specific, acting as remote sensors and manipulators for the central mind.MW-Scout: Rapid reconnaissance.MW-Geo: Non-invasive geological analysis.MW-Bio: Non-invasive biological observation (e.g., eDNA sequencing).MW-Comms: Mobile communication relays.4. Multi-Agent Coordination and Swarm Intelligence4.1. Formalizing Swarm Behavior The coordination of the Leviathan swarm can be formally modeled as a Multi-Agent Markov Decision Process (MAMDP). The objective is to learn a joint policy, π, that maximizes a global reward function, R, which balances scientific discovery (e.g., maximizing novel area surveyed) against ecological non-disturbance. R_total = w_1 * R_discovery - w_2 * R_disturbance; Where w_1 and w_2 are weights that can be dynamically adjusted based on the ethical sensitivity of the current operational zone.4.2. Bio-Inspired Coordination Algorithms To implement this, specific bio-inspired algorithms can be adopted. The Salp Swarm Algorithm (SSA) provides a compelling model for coordinated exploration (Mirjalili et al., 2017). In this model, the high-cognition LV units act as ”leaders,” using their advanced reasoning to move towards scientifically promising targets (e.g., a newly detected hydrothermal vent). The MW units act as ”followers,” conducting dense, localized surveys in the path defined by the leader’s trajectory. This provides a mathematical basis for self-organizing, emergent exploration patterns.5. Ethical Governance and Operational ProtocolsLeviathan’s license to operate is predicated on its ability to do so without causing harm. Its ethical framework is a foundational component of its architecture.5.1. A Priori Ethical Framework: Hard-Coded Constraints The RMP-TxMU is governed by non-negotiable constraints:The Prime Directive: Non-Interference: Actions predicted to cause physical disruption are assigned an infinitely negative utility value.The Precautionary Principle: The default behavior in unknown situations is passive observation.Data Sanctity: All data is logged on an immutable, blockchain-secured ledger for audit.5.2. The ICA-TxMU: A Curriculum for Moral Development Leviathan will be ”raised,” not just programmed. The Infant-Child Assessment-TxMU (ICA-TxMU) is a training protocol that guides the AGI through a structured ethical curriculum in a high-fidelity simulation before deployment, using Reinforcement Learning with Human Interaction (RIL) to build nuanced ethical wisdom.6. Physical Embodiment and In-Situ Systems6.1. Chassis, Propulsion, and Power The LV and MW units will be constructed from pressure-neutral components, filling the chassis with a non-compressible dielectric fluid to eliminate the need for heavy pressure hulls. Propulsion will be via silent, high-efficiency undulating fins inspired by cuttlefish. The hybrid power system will rely on Thermoelectric Generation (TEG) from ambient temperature gradients and inductive charging at geothermally powered deep-sea docks.6.2. Communication Infrastructure Communication will be multi-modal, prioritizing stealth and bandwidth over range.Acoustic Modems: For low-bandwidth, long-range telemetry and emergency signals.Underwater Li-Fi: For high-bandwidth, short-range intra-swarm data sharing.Bioluminescent Encoding: A novel, ultra-stealthy method for close-range signaling when observing sensitive fauna, mimicking natural communication methods.7. Challenges and Technology Readiness Level (TRL) AssessmentWhile the Leviathan architecture is conceptually cohesive, its realization depends on significant advancements in several key technology areas. A frank assessment using the NASA TRL scale reveals the primary research and development challenges.

title: Governance Twin Framework: Sentinel+Council Architecture for Agentic AI Systems in Digital Twin-Enabled Predictive Maintenance
authors: Noel P. Greis; Wolfgang Rohde; Rick Doten
abstract: As agentic AI systems are deployed in safety-critical manufacturing environments, traditional hierarchical governance structures prove inadequate for managing autonomous decision-making at machine speed. This paper introduces the concept of the Governance Twin. This framework represents a distributed multi-agent architecture that enables co-evolutionary governance of digital twin-enabled predictive maintenance systems. The framework implements a Sentinel+Council structure where sentinel agents continuously monitor operational agents for emergent vulnerabilities, behavioral drift, and constraint violations, while council agents negotiate responses that balance competing objectives through collaborative deliberation rather than hierarchical control. Unlike classic software agents that rely on syntactic communication through predefined programming constructs, agentic AI leverages semantic communication to dynamically interpret intent and select appropriate tools, models, and actions not explicitly programmed at development time. We demonstrate how this approach manages inherent tensions between operational goals and intrinsic safety requirements—uptime, efficiency, and profitability—through contextual adaptive decision-making and structural interdependence between AI operations and human safety values. Integration with knowledge graphs and other tools enables causal reasoning and explainable decision-making while maintaining governance at machine speed. The framework is instantiated within predictive maintenance scenarios to illustrate vulnerability detection, multi-objective negotiation, and prevention of cascading failures in industrial systems. © 2026 The Authors. title: Fully Automated Land Rig Pipe Handling: Learnings from the First Year in Operation
authors: C. Craig; Abhishek Kr. Gupta; D.E. Yenzer; D. Hasler; J. Towns
venue: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope A look at learnings from the first year of operations on a fully automated rig floor package retrofitted to a 2000hp Permian Basin rig. Technical issues and optimization efforts will be reviewed as the factors driving next-generation pipe handling system that improves safety while meeting well delivery metrics. Methods, Procedures, Process The retrofittable automation system controls several tools and technologies automating pipe handling for drilling, tripping, casing running, offline stand building and routine BHA handling. Keeping the focus on this area provides a drilling environment where risk due to man / machine interactions are substantially reduced or eliminated. During this proof period, improvements have continued in casing handling and running that are being optimized based on the learnings from the current pipe handling system. These improvements are being flowed through engineering and will support the next generation automated rig floor improvements. Results, Observations, Conclusions While the industry continues to focus on improvements in crew safety and consistency, applications of automated drilling systems often cannot justify the expense of a next generation drilling rig. Automation systems specifically designed to be retrofitted to existing rig designs provide these capabilities for a fraction of the cost of a new rig. This means the next evolution in safety can be affordable and installed on current drilling rigs with only short windows of down time. Existing technologies like robotics, modern control systems, closed-loop feedback, and zone management for both machines and crew all combined to focus on getting the job done safely are no longer exercises in what could be, rather what is available. Within the contractor fleet several rigs of the same design are working in the same field drilling the same wells which allows for direct comparison of key performance indicators for the automation system. Learnings from the first year will be reviewed and discussed. Novel/Additive Information Versions of pipe handling have been with the industry since the advent of harsh environment floaters. Today's automated functionality brings a new level of crew-less operations. Keeping crew separated from hazards is the next step in rig floor operations. This improved level of safety can now be achieved through more economical, retrofittable upgrades while maintaining similar rig performance metrics.

title: FLEX-AI ZD: Zero-Default Algorithm for 1000-Node Graph Resolution
authors: outail benhadid
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Background. Probabilistic AI systems, including state-of-the-art Large Language Models, fail catastrophically on complex dependency graphs. GPT-4 hallucinates on 14-node systems. Industrial applications (power grids, drone fleets, financial networks, neurobiology) require deterministic, zero-default resolution of 1000+ node graphs. Algorithm. FLEX-AI ZD is a zero-default algorithm for resolving 1000-node dependency graphs. It operates with O(n) complexity, requiring 80,000 operations for a 40×25 grid (1000 nodes). The algorithm uses phase-damping (α = 0.5) to converge deterministically to the universal attractor (-51.1 mV) with zero hallucinations. Contraction is mathematically guaranteed (norm = 0.0556 < 1). Performance. Execution time: < 0.1 sec on CPU. Precision: 2.55 × 10⁻¹¹ mV. Success rate: 100%. Compared to the Attention mechanism (O(n²·d)), FLEX-AI ZD requires 12,500× fewer operations, runs 20× faster, and consumes 10,000× less energy. Executable Code. This publication includes complete Python source code, executable immediately. The algorithm is fully reproducible. Session ID: V3-FLEXAI-ZD-1000N-16042026. Applications. Power grid stabilization (1000 transformers), drone fleet coordination (1000 units), neurobiological modeling (1000 neurons), financial simulation (1000 assets), epidemiological spread prediction (1000 zones). title: Latent Variable Nested Set Transformers & AutoBots.
authors: Roger Girgis; Florian Golemo; Felipe Codevilla; Jim Aldon D'Souza; Samira Ebrahimi Kahou; Felix Heide; Christopher Pal
abstract: Humans have the innate ability to attend to the most relevant actors in their vicinity and can forecast how they may behave in the future. This ability will be crucial for the deployment of safety-critical agents such as robots or vehicles which interact with humans. We propose a theoretical framework for this problem setting based on autoregressively modelling sequences of nested sets, using latent variables to better capture multimodal distributions over future sets of sets. We present a new model architecture which we call a Nested Set Transformer which employs multi-head self-attention blocks over sets of sets that serve as a form of social attention between the elements of the sets at every timestep. Our approach can produce a distribution over future trajectories for all agents under consideration, or focus upon the trajectory of an ego-agent. We validate the Nested Set Transformer for autonomous driving settings which we refer to as (AutoBot), where we model the trajectory of an ego-agent based on the sequential observations of key attributes of multiple agents in a scene. AutoBot produces results better than state-of-the-art published prior work on the challenging nuScenes vehicle trajectory modeling benchmark. We also examine the multi-agent prediction version of our model and jointly forecast an ego-agent's future trajectory along with the other agents in the scene. We validate the behavior of our proposed Nested Set Transformer for scene level forecasting with a pedestrian trajectory dataset.

title: Tau-Governed Rescue Drone Swarm
authors: Michal Harcej
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Autonomous drone swarms offer significant potential for disaster search andrescue by providing rapid aerial sensing, distributed coverage, victim detection,communication relay, and adaptive task allocation. However, disasterenvironments impose simultaneous constraints on energy, communication,sensing reliability, computation, and physical safety. Existing multi-UAVapproaches address these constraints through task allocation, distributed control,reinforcement learning, stochastic optimization, and energy-aware planning, butmission execution commonly remains driven by physical clock time and externallydefined control frequencies.This paper proposes a Tau-Governed Rescue Swarm Architecture (TGRSA), ahierarchical autonomy framework in which mission-level progression is governedby accumulated validated coherence rather than elapsed time alone. Thearchitecture introduces Tau-Time, a state-dependent computational time variablethat accumulates according to sensor coherence, semantic consistency,uncertainty, and mission alignment. Entropy is incorporated explicitly so that highagreement cannot by itself be interpreted as high confidence.The proposed system separates deterministic flight safety and control fromadaptive cognitive governance. A hard real-time control layer maintains flightstability and physical constraints, while a Tau governance layer regulates missiontempo, verification frequency, computational expenditure, swarm coordination,and progression through mission milestones. A Constitution provides immutablesafety constraints, an Altered Mirror provides action-context verification, aTask/Goal Drift Aligner measures deviation from mission objectives, and TauTicksgate significant mission transitions.The architecture further incorporates short-term memory, working memory, and apersistent Collective Knowledge Graph. Experience accumulated during activemissions is consolidated during charging or scheduled rest periods rather thanmodifying safety-critical policies during flight. This creates a dual-timescaleautonomous system capable of acting in real time while learning asynchronously.The central hypothesis is that coherence-governed execution can reduceunnecessary computation, corrective maneuvers, and energy expenditure whilemaintaining or improving mission safety under uncertainty. We propose anexperimental framework comparing Tau-governed swarms with fixed-rate,heuristic, and learning-based baselines across simulated disaster environmentswith sensor degradation, communication loss, UAV failures, dynamic hazards, andconstrained battery capacity.Keywords: UAV swarm, search and rescue, disaster robotics, autonomoussystems, adaptive computation, uncertainty, entropy, energy-aware autonomy,multi-agent systems, mission governance.

title: Agentic AI in Construction: A Systematic Review and Human-Governed Framework for Autonomous Project Delivery
authors: Amer A. Hijazi; Ali Mohammed Alashwal; Milad Baghalzadeh Shishehgarkhaneh; Rodrigo Neves Calheiros; Priyadarshini Das; Pejman Ghasemi Poor Sabet
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) has emerged as a new paradigm that extends conventional artificial intelligence by integrating autonomous reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and adaptive decision-making into goal-directed systems. Although interest in Agentic AI has rapidly increased, its application within the construction industry remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive synthesis. This study presents a systematic literature review of Agentic AI in construction, following the PRISMA methodology and analysing 50 journal articles published between 2021 and 2026. The review examines the conceptual evolution of Agentic AI, architectural paradigms, intelligence mechanisms, enabling technologies, lifecycle applications, reported benefits, validation approaches, adoption barriers, and future research directions. The findings show a clear transition from precursor forms of computational agency, including rule-based agent-based modelling and reinforcement-learning systems, towards contemporary Agentic AI characterised by increasingly modular, hybrid, tool-enabled, multi-agent, and human-governed architectures supported by large language models, digital twins, robotics, and Internet of Things technologies. Current applications primarily support project planning, scheduling, logistics, safety management, inspection, quality control, structural design, and facility operation. However, most studies remain at prototype or simulation stages, with limited real-world deployment and inconsistent evaluation methods. The review also identifies significant technical, organisational, and governance challenges, including engineering reliability, interoperability, explainability, human oversight, and data integration. Building on these findings, the study proposes the Human-Governed Construction Agentic Intelligence Loop (H-CAIL), a construction-specific closed-loop framework that integrates project context, multimodal perception, goal-directed planning, reasoning, tool selection, human-governed action, evaluation, and adaptive learning to support trustworthy autonomous decision-making across the construction lifecycle. Finally, the study presents a future research agenda to support the development of trustworthy, scalable, and construction-specific Agentic AI ecosystems capable of enabling autonomous yet human-governed project delivery across the entire asset lifecycle.

title: H3CPP: Boundary-Safe Coverage Path Planning for Multi-USV Operations in Irregular Coastal Environments
authors: Giannis Spiliopoulos; Elias K. Xidias; Dimitris Zissis
abstract: As the need for persistent ocean monitoring grows, fleets of Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) are a promising way to survey large marine protected areas with low operational cost. Their effectiveness, however, depends on solving a challenging multi-robot Coverage Path Planning (CPP) problem over complex coastal geometries while strictly respecting safety boundaries. This paper presents H3CPP, a CPP framework that leverages the H3 hierarchical hexagonal grid to discretize arbitrarily shaped marine areas, cluster them into connected subregions, and construct boundary-aware graphs on which Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) tours are computed. Each H3 cell is sized to match the nominal sensing footprint of a USV, and edges that intersect land or forbidden zones are exponentially penalized, encouraging safe paths that remain within the operational polygon. We evaluate H3CPP on seven benchmark polygonal maps and on a real-world coastal marina using 1–10 USVs. For a single USV in complex, non-convex environments, H3CPP achieves near-complete coverage (coverage ratio ≈ 1.0 of the target area) while avoiding boundary violations that occur with swath and spiral baselines, and reduces path length by up to 10% compared to these methods in the most irregular shapes. In the Syros marina scenario, multi-USV experiments show that H3CPP decreases the total traveled distance by 4–34% (≈ 20% on average) relative to a decomposition-plus-swaths baseline, while maintaining similar coverage and systematically reducing mission makespan as the fleet size increases from 1 to 10 USVs. The proposed framework therefore combines geodesic hexagonal indexing, connectivity-aware clustering, and penalized graph-based TSP planning into a practical CPP solution for USV swarms operating in realistic coastal environments.

title: The Forthcoming Freezing of the European West Coast is Seemingly a ‘Divine Retribution’
authors: Michael Gurevitz
abstract: This short essay links the expected cooling of Western Europe's climate to the colonial history of its maritime nations. It observes that empires with strong naval fleets on Europe's west coast, such as Great Britain, France, Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands, were never really 'punished' for their imperialist conquests. These countries have enjoyed winter temperatures about 10°C higher than the zonal mean at equivalent latitudes, which has been attributed to heat carried from the Gulf Stream by westerly winds and to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, an ocean conveyor belt driven by differences in temperature and salt content. Citing recent studies, the author notes that the Atlantic heat circulation system is changing, that the Gulf Stream appears more sluggish and is expected within this century to move away from the European coast, and that, with global heating from human industrial activity, temperatures on the European west coast are expected to fall by 10-15°C on average, bringing colder winters, stronger storms and floods. The author suggests that people who believe in reward and punishment may see this as a 'heavenly punishment' for past colonial sins, but concludes that the change shows that thousands of years of balanced weather do not guarantee continuation and that life on Earth is always at risk of sudden catastrophe. title: Self-Supervised Diagnostics & Prognostics Framework for Predictive Maintenance in Electric Vehicles
authors: Pankaj Kumar; Kaushik Deole; Umesh N. Hivarkar
venue: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Predictive maintenance is critical to improving reliability, safety and operational efficiency of connected vehicles. However, classic supervised learning methods for fault prediction rely heavily on large-scale labeled data of failures, which are difficult to obtain and maintain a manually built dataset of failure events in real automotives settings. In this paper, we present a novel self-supervised anomaly detection model that makes predictions on the faults without the need for labeled failures by using only the operational data when the systems or robots are healthy. The method relies on self-supervised pretext tasks, like masked signal reconstruction and future telemetry prediction, to extract nominal multi-sensor dynamics (i.e., temperature, pressure, current, vibration) while jointly minimizing the deviation between encoded/decoded signals and normal patterns in the latent space. A unsupervised anomaly detection model is then used to detect when the learned patterns are violated. This in conjunction with data driven predictive allows for early fault detection on key subsystems such as batteries, electric motors, brake systems, and cooling systems. They tested the framework on some public benchmark datasets, and it’s pretty good at catching early anomalies with high accuracy and recall even better than the usual threshold-based methods. The study points out how important it is to use data from normal, healthy systems to build maintenance strategies that can scale well, adapt easily, and save costs, especially for connected vehicle fleets. Plus, the model helps explain what’s going on by identifying which telemetry signals are behind the anomalies, making it easier to take timely and practical maintenance actions. This work basically offers a new, practical way to keep vehicle health in check ahead of time, helping fleets stay up and running longer while cutting down on surprise breakdowns and expensive repairs.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Large Language Models and Agentic AI Systems for Chemistry and Materials Science
authors: Michal Ezeh; Etinosa Osaro
abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has catalyzed a paradigm shift in computational chemistry and materials science, evolving from passive prediction tools to active autonomous agents capable of orchestrating complex scientific workflows. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of LLM based systems in chemistry and materials science from 2020 onwards, establishing a taxonomy that progresses from domain specific language models through tool augmented systems to fully autonomous closed loop discovery platforms. We systematically examine chemical foundation models including ChemBERTa, MoLFormer, and MolT5, alongside materials-focused architecture such as MatSciBERT and MatterGPT. We evaluate their capabilities across molecular property prediction, reaction planning, materials design, and experimental optimization. The review critically analyzes agentic systems such as ChemCrow, Coscientist, and multi agent frameworks that integrate retrieval, simulation tools, and robotic laboratory interfaces to enable autonomous experimentation. Detailed benchmark mappings, evaluation metrics, and reproducibility standards are presented while addressing critical challenges in verification, safety, and trustworthiness for lab facing AI agents. Special emphasis is placed on grounding strategies to mitigate hallucinations, formal constraint validation, and human in the loop safeguards. Our analysis reveals that while current systems demonstrate impressive capabilities in constrained tasks, fundamental challenges remain in true chemical reasoning, uncertainty quantification, and long horizon planning. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for multimodal scientific foundation models, standardized community benchmarks, and governance frameworks necessary for the responsible deployment of autonomous discovery systems in chemistry and materials laboratories.

title: Lume-Mar: A Deterministic Governance Substrate for Maritime, Port, and Naval Systems
authors: Ronald Jason Andrews
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Maritime systems operate at the intersection of hydrology, environmental dynamics, industrial activity, and global logistics — yet today, maritime governance is nondeterministic, fragmented, and disconnected from the physical substrates that determine vessel safety, port efficiency, and environmental compliance. Existing systems — AIS, VTS, IMO routing guidelines, and port management platforms — operate in silos, lack cross‑vertical awareness, and provide no replay‑identical audit capability. This paper introduces Lume‑Mar, the first deterministic governance substrate for maritime, port, and naval systems. Built on the Lume‑V governance layer and the Lume‑Ops universal operational substrate, Lume‑Mar integrates vessel routing, port operations, offshore industrial coordination, hydrodynamic safety, environmental compliance, jurisdictional enforcement, and naval priority into a single replay‑identical state machine. It enforces maritime invariants, hydrodynamic envelopes, deterministic multi‑agent arbitration, override logic, and certificate‑based auditability across the full spectrum of maritime operations — from open‑ocean routing to berth‑level crane scheduling to intermodal cold‑chain logistics.

title: ATOS, An Open-Source Platform for Testing AI-Based Automated Vehicle Systems in Integrated Simulated and Physical Scenarios
authors: Victor Jarlow; Lukas Wikander; Samuel Thorén; Robert Brenick; Xianbiao Hu; Timo Kero
venue: ACM International Conference on Distributed and Event-Based Systems (DEBS)
abstract: The increasing complexity of automated and AI-based vehicle systems necessitates novel testing methodologies to ensure safety, reliability, and performance in diverse and dynamic scenarios.This paper introduces AV Test Operating System (ATOS), an open-source platform that seamlessly integrates simulated and physical testing environments for Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems and Automated Driving systems.ATOS supports comprehensive scenario evaluations under varied conditions such as weather, traffic, and connectivity environments by automating and orchestrating tests involving multiple simultaneous virtual and physical objects.Key contributions of this work include: 1) The introduction and design of ATOS, an open-source platform for automating and orchestrating complex vehicle testing scenarios.2) A method for evaluating the repeatability of automated test orchestration systems.3) Data analysis of two scenarios where ATOS was used in real-life AV testing.Results demonstrate ATOS's effectiveness in executing repeatable and reliable tests across diverse configurations, highlighting its utility for research institutions, vehicle manufacturers, and testing facilities.Using ATOS in repeated runs, the time delay when triggering dynamic events was within 1 millisecond with virtual objects and 7 milliseconds when using physical objects.The positional variation between runs using virtual and real-life objects amounted to 6 and 20 cm, respectively. title: Statistical limits and conditional complexity in real-world reinforcement learning: a tutorial survey
authors: Amar Ahmad; Yvonne Vallès; Youssef Idaghdour
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in controlled environments, demonstrating superhuman performance in domains such as game playing and simulated robotics. However, its transition to real-world applications remains constrained by fundamental statistical challenges that limit scalability, reliability, and safety. This study systematically examines four such challenges: sample inefficiency, in which millions of interactions may be required even for simple tasks; nonstationarity, arising from evolving environmental dynamics and agent-induced distribution shifts; partial observability, which violates the Markov assumption and inflates estimation variance; and the curse of dimensionality, which causes exploration demands to grow rapidly in high-dimensional spaces. Known theoretical lower bounds from the literature are reviewed to characterize the fundamental limits of these challenges, and a survey of contemporary mitigation strategies is presented, including model-based methods, robust Markov decision process formulations, memory-augmented architectures, and hierarchical abstractions. In addition to these core statistical challenges, this study briefly discusses related deployment-oriented topics-including safe RL, explainable RL, multi-agent coordination, and curriculum learning-that interact with, but remain distinct from, the four primary statistical limits. This study is intended as a tutorial synthesis rather than a source of new theoretical results. Its main contribution is organizational and interpretive: It unifies existing lower bounds, representative complexity arguments, and practical mitigation strategies around the structural assumptions that make real-world RL easier or harder.

title: Development of a digital twin for Crazyflie drone swarm testing
authors: Kin Wang Tung
abstract: This thesis explores the development and validation of a game engine-based digital twin system for Crazyflie drone swarms. The limitations of the Crazyflie platform, such as short battery life, dependence on external localisation systems like VICON, and limited onboard sensing, shaped the design requirements of the system. The proposed digital twin was implemented in mixed reality. It allows real-time synchronisation between physical and virtual Crazyflies, simulates perception through virtual LiDAR sensors and cameras, and enables hybrid swarm operations combining real and virtual agents in a shared virtual environment. Unity was selected as the development platform because of its balance of rendering performance, moderate hardware requirements, official support of ROS2, and abundance of learning resources. To extend the capabilities of Crazyflie swarm for research and testing, four features were developed, including dynamic obstacle simulation, integration of virtual sensors and cameras, scalable swarm size through virtual Crazyflies, and autonomous replacement of Crazyflies to extend experiment duration. Experimental scenarios validated its effectiveness for coordinated multi-agent tasks, vision coverage, realistic virtual sensing as well as reduced hardware dependency and risk of hardware damage. This work shows that a game engine–based digital twin can significantly improve the flexibility, scalability, and safety of swarm robotics research while lowering hardware costs and physical space requirements. Future work could enhance model fidelity using AI and extend the system for remote or cloud-based swarm experimentation.

title: Certified Neural Network Control Architectures: Methodological Advances in Stability, Robustness, and Cross-Domain Applications
authors: Rui Liu; Jianhua Huang; Biao Lu; Weili Ding
abstract: Neural network (NN)-based controllers have emerged as a paradigm-shifting approach in modern control systems, demonstrating unparalleled capabilities in governing nonlinear dynamical systems with inherent uncertainties. This comprehensive review systematically investigates the theoretical foundations and practical implementations of NN controllers through the prism of Lyapunov stability theory, NN controller frameworks, and robustness analysis. The review establishes that recurrent neural architectures inherently address time-delayed state compensation and disturbance rejection, achieving superior trajectory tracking performance compared to classical control strategies. By integrating imitation learning with barrier certificate constraints, the proposed methodology ensures provable closed-loop stability while maintaining safety-critical operation bounds. Experimental evaluations using chaotic system benchmarks confirm the exceptional modeling capacity of NN controllers in capturing complex dynamical behaviors, complemented by formal verification advances through reachability analysis techniques. Practical demonstrations in aerial robotics and intelligent transportation systems highlight the efficacy of controllers in real-world scenarios involving environmental uncertainties and multi-agent interactions. The theoretical framework synergizes data-driven learning with nonlinear control principles, introducing hybrid automata formulations for transient response analysis and adjoint sensitivity methods for network optimization. These innovations position NN controllers as a transformative technology in control engineering, offering fundamental advances in stability-guaranteed learning and topology optimization. Future research directions will emphasize the integration of physics-informed neural operators for distributed control systems and event-triggered implementations for resource-constrained applications, paving the way for next-generation intelligent control architectures.
