title: Constraint-First Governance for Robust AI Search and Agentic Systems
authors: Mark Anthony Brewer
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Constraint-First Governance for Robust AI Search and Agentic Systems Classification: PUBLIC-SAFE(Architectural principles only. No operational thresholds, enforcement logic, or reconstruction methods are disclosed.) 1. Purpose This document describes a governance-first architectural pattern for large-scale AI systems operating across search, synthesis, and agentic workflows. Its purpose is to explain why certain classes of AI failure emerge at scale and what kind of governance abstractions are required to prevent them—without disclosing implementation details, enforcement mechanisms, or operational parameters. This paper is descriptive, not prescriptive. 2. Scope This paper applies to AI systems that: operate across multiple domains or modalities integrate search or external tools generate synthesized conclusions rather than single responses participate in decision-support or delegated action workflows must maintain coherence across time and context Examples include (non-exhaustive): search-integrated assistants multi-agent reasoning systems enterprise AI orchestration platforms research and analysis copilots 3. Explicit Public-Safety Boundary This document does not include: enforcement thresholds rejection criteria convergence deadlines reconstruction pipelines physics-informed validation methods dual-use implementation logic any instructions that would enable replication Where necessary, such mechanisms are referenced only as abstract classes, not as procedures. 4. The Core Problem As AI systems scale, failures increasingly arise not from lack of intelligence, but from lack of governed authority. Observed failure modes include: internally consistent but externally incorrect conclusions escalation of exploratory reasoning into authoritative claims search relevance overpowering constraint validity inability to halt synthesis before unsafe convergence loss of identity consistency across contexts These are control failures, not model failures. 5. Key Design Premise Intelligence without governance does not fail loudly.It fails coherently. Therefore, robustness at scale requires constraint-first governance, not additional prediction capacity. 6. Definitions (Public-Safe) Constraint: A boundary that limits allowable system states without prescribing outcomes. Drift: Divergence between internally coherent reasoning and externally lawful configurations. Authority: The permission for an output to be treated as settled, durable, or actionable. Silence: A valid system outcome when constraints do not converge. 7. What This Paper Claims—and What It Does Not This paper claims: certain governance patterns improve robustness when present certain failure modes are predictable under scale certain abstractions are necessary for safe agentic behavior This paper does not claim: universality exclusivity superiority over any specific system completeness or finality 8. Reader Guidance This document should be read as: an architectural lens a design vocabulary a risk-containment framework It is not a blueprint. WHY PREDICTION-ONLY SYSTEMS FAIL AT SCALE 9. The Scaling Illusion Early AI systems appear to improve monotonically as: data volume increases, model size grows, and inference speed accelerates. This creates a scaling illusion: the belief that more intelligence automatically yields more correctness. At small scale, this appears true.At system scale, it fails. 10. The Fundamental Limitation of Prediction Prediction-centric systems optimize for: likelihood, relevance, and internal consistency. They do not optimize for: lawfulness, safety, or long-term coherence across contexts. As a result, prediction-only systems tend to: reinforce early hypotheses overweight frequent but incorrect patterns converge on confident falsehoods mistake internal agreement for truth This failure mode becomes worse, not better, as systems grow. 11. The Difference Between Intelligence and Authority A critical distinction often goes unmodeled: Intelligence = the ability to generate plausible states Authority = permission for a state to persist, propagate, or act Prediction systems excel at the first.They have no native concept of the second. Without explicit governance, systems begin to: treat exploratory reasoning as settled output, collapse uncertainty prematurely, and propagate error with increasing confidence. 12. Search as a Drift Amplifier When prediction is combined with search and retrieval: relevance ranking can outweigh constraint validity correlated sources reinforce each other speculative narratives gain apparent legitimacy This produces epistemic drift: outputs that are internally coherent but externally invalid. Notably, this drift often looks like success: fluent language, rich citations, confident tone. Which is why it is dangerous. 13. Why Human Oversight Alone Is Insufficient Relying solely on human review fails at scale because: humans encounter outputs after synthesis reviewers cannot reconstruct full reasoning paths fatigue and trust creep distort judgment systems operate faster than oversight loops Governance must be structural, not reactive. 14. The Emergence of Agentic Risk As systems move from: answering → planning → acting, the cost of error increases sharply. In agentic workflows: a single incorrect assumption can cascade intermediate reasoning is often hidden rollback is difficult or impossible At this point, permission to act becomes more important than ability to reason. 15. The Core Insight At scale, the dominant failure mode of AI is not lack of intelligence,but lack of stopping rules. This paper argues that: prediction must be subordinated to governance, intelligence must be bounded by constraint, and authority must be explicitly granted, not assumed. 16. Implication for System Design Any AI system that: synthesizes across domains, persists across contexts, or participates in action loops, requires a governance layer that operates independently of model prediction. This layer answers a different question: “Is this output allowed to settle or act?”not“Is this output likely?” CONSTRAINT-FIRST GOVERNANCE: FROM HEURISTICS TO INVARIANTS 17. Why Heuristics Break Under Pressure Most governance mechanisms in AI today rely on heuristics: policy checklists content filters confidence thresholds red-teaming feedback loops post-hoc moderation Heuristics work when: domains are narrow, stakes are low, and errors are reversible. They fail when: domains interact, systems persist across time, or actions have real-world consequences. This failure is structural, not incidental. 18. Constraints vs. Rules A key distinction: Rules prescribe behavior. Constraints limit the space of allowable behavior. Rules must be updated continually.Constraints remain stable across changing conditions. Constraint-first systems: do not predict the future, they bound what futures are allowed. This difference is critical for governance at scale. 19. Why Constraints Scale When Policies Do Not Policies are human artifacts: language-dependent, context-sensitive, and vulnerable to interpretation drift. Constraints operate at the system level: independent of phrasing, invariant under scale, enforceable without interpretation. As systems grow, only constraints remain legible. 20. Constraint Closure as a Stability Requirement For governance to be effective, constraints must be: explicit persistent mutually reinforcing When constraints are closed under system operations: drift is bounded, identity is preserved, and failure modes become detectable. This closure is a design requirement, not a philosophical stance. 21. Authority as a Derived Property In a constraint-first architecture: authority is not assumed, authority is derived from compliance with constraints. An output becomes authoritative only if: it satisfies the current constraint set, and does not violate system invariants. Otherwise, the correct outcome is: provisional output, deferred judgment, or silence. 22. Silence as a Lawful Outcome A constraint-first system must allow: non-answers, unresolved states, and explicit uncertainty. Silence is not failure.Silence is containment. This property prevents: premature convergence, false certainty, and unsafe escalation. 23. Why Constraint-First Governance Is Model-Agnostic Because constraints govern authority, not generation: they can sit above any model, operate across heterogeneous agents, and remain independent of training data. This allows: compatibility with existing systems, incremental adoption, and non-disruptive integration. 24. The Shift From Optimization to Preservation Traditional AI optimizes for: performance, accuracy, or efficiency. Constraint-first governance optimizes for: coherence over time, safety under uncertainty, identity preservation across contexts. This shift is necessary when systems persist beyond single interactions. 25. Design Implication Any AI system intended to: coordinate agents, manage knowledge over time, or participate in decisions, must encode: constraints as first-class entities, authority as conditional, and stopping as a valid state. title: Ambient air pollution in China
authors: Guang‐Hui Dong
abstract: Ambient air pollution is a global problem of increasing concern to governments and the public. Air pollution causes more than 4.2 million deaths annually, and this figure is likely to exceed 6.3 million deaths by 2050 unless there is a significant intervention.1 As the world's largest developing country, China's rapid economic growth has come at a cost of dangerous ambient air pollution, which threatens human health and sustainable social and economic development. Rapid industrialization and urbanization over the last three decades in China has created one of the highest disease burdens in the world. In 2017, 81% of Chinese people were living in places where PM2.5 (particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5μm) concentrations were higher than the Interim Target-1 limit (35 μg/m3) set by the World Health Organization (WHO), and 50% of Chinese people were exposed to annual-average PM2.5 concentrations of >48.2 μg/m3.2 China has the world's second largest economy and many sources of harmful emissions when compared to other developed countries (e.g. USA and Europe). China consumes roughly 50% of the world's coal due to outdated technology and poorly maintained coal facilities. The number of on-road vehicles adds to this burden, as the civilian fleet has increased from 16 million vehicles in 2000 to 229 million vehicles in 2018. China's widespread industrial development, coal-dependent energy utilization and vast number of personal vehicles have led to compound air pollution which is a blend of coal smoke and motor vehicle emissions. What health impacts does this ambient air pollution have on the population of China? For a large majority of the exposed population, disease burden and economic loss due to ambient air pollution in China are greater than in other countries. For example, according to economic loss calculations estimated using the Global Burden of Disease framework, ambient air pollution is the fifth leading risk factor for all-cause disease mortality in China and caused 1.1 million deaths in 2015, which contributes to 26% of estimated deaths associated with air pollution globally.3 According to the China Pulmonary Health Study,4 8.6% of the Chinese population (or nearly 100 million people) have chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and 18.7% of total COPD deaths can be attributed to ambient PM2.5 exposure.2 However, it may be more meaningful and informative to compare mortality associated with ambient air pollution with cigarette smoking habits. For example, as a standard, one cigarette per day is roughly equivalent to 22 μg/m3 of PM2.5. In 2015, Beijing had pollution levels at about 85 μg/m3 of PM2.5 which was equivalent to roughly four cigarettes per day. Whereas in 2016, levels of PM2.5 in Beijing shot to 550 μg/m3, equivalent to 25 cigarettes per day for every man, woman and child living in the city. Taking into consideration the nonlinear exposure–effect relationship between air pollution and health effects, along with the unique socio-demographic characteristics of China (e.g. age structure, disease pattern and socio-economic status), studies pertaining to Chinese subjects may provide a better understanding about the role of potential modifiers of adverse health effects of ambient air pollution (Fig. 1). For example, in 2013, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), a branch of the WHO, conducted a meta-analyses of 18 studies to examine the exposure–effect relationship of ambient particulate matter (PM) and found that the meta-relative risk for lung cancer was 1.09 (95% CI: 1.04–1.14) for PM2.5 and 1.08 (95% CI: 1.00–1.17) for PM10 (particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter ≤10μm), per 10 μg/m3 increase in exposure to PM.5 However, most of these 18 studies were from regions of North America and Europe, with only one study from China. Furthermore, the only study in China was conducted 20 years ago using total suspended particulate (TSP) concentrations to estimate levels of PM2.5 exposure. So, this exposure–effect relationship reported from IARC does not accurately depict the effects of air pollution in China. The results from the China Four Cities Study, a 12-year retrospective cohort of 39 054 participants, showed that each 10 μg/m3 increase in PM10 concentration was associated with a 65% (95% CI: 1.527–1.791) increase in lung cancer mortality,6 which was higher than those reported from IARC, indicating that findings based on Chinese populations are essential to understand and improve the assessment of the global health hazards of air pollution. In recent years, China has made substantial progress in reducing air pollution, and monitoring data show that national average PM2.5 concentrations decreased by 46% from 72 μg/m3 in 2013 to 39 μg/m3 in 2018.7 However, prevention and control of air pollution seems to have decreased, due to the government's low priority for environmental issues, lack of cooperation among various agencies and most of all inadequate government funding. In this context, China has developed strict environmental regulations such as the newly enacted China Air Pollution Prevention and Control Law that holds the local government responsible for areas under its administration for a cleaner and better environment. However, local government may not be the most suitable agency to deliver and enforce change, as no clear set of guidelines are present on how to implement the policy. It is not clear what to do and who should be accountable if air quality standards are not implemented. Furthermore, rural areas of China are also facing great challenges in migration and diffusion of air pollutants due to the transfer of highly polluting industries from central cities to suburban or rural districts. This transfer may cause much more serious environmental pollution due to the lack of supervision in rural areas. To correct this problem, in 2018, the 'Ministry of Ecology and Environment' was established to formulate policies to achieve environmental protection on a national scale using statutory power. The current status of China as one of the major global polluters makes the success of these initiatives of great importance, with the overall goal of improving human health alongside sustainable social and economic growth. This work was supported by National Key Research and Development Program of China (2016YFC0207000) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (81872582).

title: TetraKlein: A Unified Architecture

abstract: TetraKlein is a unified computational, cryptographic, and extended-reality (XR) architecture developed by Baramay Station Research Inc., a Canadian non-profit research organization.This repository publishes the mathematical framework, AIR constraint system, XR physics formulations, digital-twin convergence rules, and verification pipeline defining the TetraKlein system. TetraKlein integrates: Post-quantum cryptography (Kyber, Dilithium, Module-LWE/SIS) Zero-knowledge proof systems (AIR, STARKs, IVC, folding, FRI) Verifiable compute engines (SP1, RISC Zero, Brevis, zkSync-derived provers) XR physics and rendering pipelines (TK-U, XR-TSU kernels, foveation models) Digital-Twin Convergence (DTC lineage, projection operators) Hypercube ledger topology (HBB, Recursive Tesseract Hashing) IPv6-native mesh identity and routing (Yggdrasil, PQC-authenticated overlays) Cross-layer AIR constraints enabling recursive multi-domain verification This repository is intended for researchers, engineers, cryptographers, XR developers, and academic institutions looking to analyze, extend, or experimentally validate a unified verifiable-compute architecture. title: The Mermaid Atoll Shipwreck-A mysterious early 19th-century loss MYRA STANBURY with 16 Contributors 307 pp., including 9 appendices, 222 figs mostly colour, 46 tables Australian National Centre of Excellence for Maritime Archaeology and the Australasian I
authors: Colin J. M. Martin
venue: The International Journal of Nautical Archaeology
abstract: The partial excavation of an early 19th-century shipwreck in a highly dynamic, shallow-water environment on a coral reef, which yielded only a few small cast-iron guns, three anchors, several ship's fittings, and a tiny collection of heavily abraded and unremarkable artefacts, might not seem to offer much prospect for a substantial archaeological report. Yet this is just what the Department of Maritime Archaeology at the Western Australian Museum—that pioneering hotbed of innovative excellence throughout our discipline's formative years—has achieved in this exemplary volume. Rowley Shoals is an isolated group of three low reefs some 300 km west of Broome, on the edge of the north-western Australian shelf, and Mermaid Reef is the most northerly of them. During exceptionally low tides in 1977, Peter Sartoria, a charter-boat skipper who ran fishing trips to the area, noted what appeared to be wreckage on the western edge of the reef's inner lagoon, and subsequently reported it to the authorities under Western Australia's enlightened historic shipwreck legislation. This triggered a response from the Museum, which, with Sartoria to transport and guide its team of maritime archaeologists, mounted a preliminary expedition to survey and assess the site in 1981. The objects on the reef turned out to be a pair of anchors, and a concentration of wreckage was located nearby in a narrow, twisting gully. This included a third anchor, a try-pot (a cast-iron cauldron for rendering whale-blubber), five iron guns, a rudder gudgeon, and various small items and ship's fittings. The size of the anchors, and general spread of wreckage, suggested that the remains were those of a ship of around 200–250 tons, while the artefact assemblage, especially the try-pot, indicated an early 19th-century date and an association with whaling. The wreck was demonstrably not, as had been considered a possibility, one of the Indonesian long-distance fishing boats known to have visited the reef complex in the pre-colonial era. Its identification, as is so often the case with shipwrecks, involved detective work in the archives. Perusal of early maps yielded what appeared to be conclusive evidence on an Admiralty Chart of 1829 that showed well to the north of the Rowley Shoals a ‘Coral Reef on which the Lively was lost’. But the location indicated is in deep water where no reef exists. It is probably a cartographic error, and the wreck on Mermaid Reef is that of the Lively, but the investigators quite properly emphasize that an element of doubt must remain. However, the name was a good starting point, and the researchers were tenacious. Lloyd's Register produced several late 18th- and early 19th-century ships of that name, but the most promising was a French-built 240-ton Lively belonging to the English whaling tycoon Daniel Bennett, which apparently failed to return to England following departure for the South Seas Fishery in November 1806. Its captain at the time was Joseph Whitehead, who evidently survived the wreck, resuming employment with Bennett in 1809. The incident therefore probably occurred around 1807–1808. This was, and remains, the most likely identification of the Mermaid Reef wreck. Once established, the French connection opened up a further and productive avenue of research that revealed that the ship had been built at Saint-Malo as the Abeille (bee) in 1765 and its initial voyage—presumably related to fishing or whaling—was to Newfoundland, which lasted almost a year. Abeille was rated at 200 tons, and carried 10 guns. In due course it became an armed transport in the service of France's fledgling Republic, and, in 1795, was taken as a prize by the British frigate Hebe. Three years later, Daniel Bennett acquired the ship for his whaling fleet and re-named it Lively. Though absolute proof of the wreck's identity remains elusive, the archaeological evidence strongly supports a French origin and an association with whaling. Three square-sectioned lead scupper-liners, which almost certainly would have been fitted when the ship was built (or, if replaced, would have been shaped to fit the original square holes), were of a distinctively French configuration. Contemporary English scuppers were round in section. The presence of iron knees, several parts of which were recovered, is less conclusive though still compatible with a French build. A total of four try-pots and a blubber-knife indicate whale processing on an industrial scale. The guns are of English pattern, and were probably obtained under Bennett's ownership when the vessel was fitting out for its long voyage to potentially contested whaling waters on the far side of the globe. No documentary source has been found to indicate the fate of the crew, although as noted above the captain, Joseph Whitehead, survived to take up later commands. However, archaeological evidence suggests that at least some of his men escaped, too. Among the relatively few small items recovered is a substantial quantity of navigational equipment, including a sounding lead and parts of at least three pairs of brass dividers—a fourth pair of graduated wing dividers was probably used for carpentry purposes. The lack of evidence for more elaborate instruments, particularly those to determine latitude and longitude, suggests that these may have been removed from the wreck. ‘Survivor salvage’ is a recognized aspect of site-formation processes, and it is quite possible that these items were taken by the survivors to navigate their passage to safety, no doubt using one or more of the catching boats that whalers carried. Following the 1982 assessment, two one-month excavation seasons, in 1983 and 1986, were conducted. The first involved Museum staff and local volunteers, while the second was supervised by Museum staff with funding and volunteers from Earthwatch. Logistically the site is not easy to work. Mermaid Atoll is entirely covered at high tide (there is a c.5 m tidal range). A base camp was set up 30 km away at Beswell Island beside the adjacent Clerke Reef, a sand cay rising 2.4 m above high water but without vegetation or fresh water. The volume describes in impressive detail the expeditionary logistics, fieldwork, historical research, and analytical studies of the finds, setting the results into wider contexts of British imperial, Australian colonial, and global history. This does not make for easy reading since the disciplines involved do not necessarily speak in similar languages, and the mental cross-referencing required to follow the often complex arguments is at times overwhelming. But helpful summaries are frequent, and it is worth reading these first, even when they come at the end of a section. Although maritime archaeology lies at its core, this is not just another wreck report. It is a major study focused on, but radiating in many directions from, a modest and apparently insignificant little wreck almost entirely destroyed by the extreme environment in which it lies. In Australian terms it is prehistoric archaeology pure and simple, covering activities along the continent's north-western coastlands two decades before formal European settlement began there. From a British perspective it relates to the long-range maritime entrepreneurship of commercial interests seeking to exploit resources in an expanding global empire. The French connection links it to the Revolutionary period and Napoleonic wars. It also sheds light on diagnostic technical differences between French and English shipbuilding associated with small quasi-vernacular vessels that, even in this comparatively late period, are less well understood than many documentarily focused historians would have us believe. And it says a great deal about formation processes and their archaeological significance in shallow high-energy zones. The principal author is Myra Stanbury, who wrote almost every chapter in conjunction with one or more of the 16 named collaborators. The exception is Ch. 12 on whaling-related artefacts, written by Jennifer Rodrigues, and some specialist aspects of the nine appendices. Illustrations are excellent and apposite, with superb photography by Patrick Baker. Many of the contributors have undertaken original research in their specialist fields, notably Ian MacLeod and his colleagues from the Museum's conservation department whose studies into historic metallurgy and conservation techniques enjoy a world-wide reputation. Academically this is a seminal volume, important not only for the original and integrated research it contains but as an exemplar of how such things should be done. It demonstrates that apparently obscure, insignificant, and unexciting shipwrecks can be as revealing and culturally valuable as a Vasa or a Mary Rose if studied by archaeologists and historians who ask the right questions and are prepared to think outside the box. More than that, it shows how an enlightened legislature, a state museum that recognizes the importance of the shipwreck heritage and how to stimulate public interest in it, and a wide community of stakeholders eager to be constructively involved can cooperate to mutual advantage. This is the framework within which Peter Sartoria was able to kick-start the whole process back in 1981, and continue supporting it without thought of monetary reward. It is good to report in conclusion that on the Museum's recommendation he received an unasked-for payment from the State at the highest level allowed.

title: Conflicting visions around technology integration: A look at recent EU drone policies
authors: Samar Abbas Nawaz
abstract: For many years, the European Commission (EC) has been envisioning integration of drones into civilian airspace. This vision entails scalable drone operations in the European civil airspace for commercial and private purposes such as inspection, urban mobility, logistics and so forth. In such regard, one finds various European declarations, strategies and regulations around civilian drones. Most recently, in late 2022, the EC adopted the 'Drone Strategy 2.0 for a Smart and Sustainable Unmanned Aircraft Eco-System in Europe' (Drone Strategy) with an aim to create a drone ecosystem for sustainable future mobility. Around half a year later, the European Union (EU) Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) passed the 'EASA AI Roadmap 2.0 Human-Centric Approach to AI in Aviation' (AI Roadmap) outlining future challenges and opportunities of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for the European aviation sector, including civilian drones. Common in both instruments is a time-bound vision: whereas the Drone Strategy envisions various facets of drone normalization to manifest in 2030, the AI Roadmap produces a timeline (2019–2050+) reflecting the planned standardization of AI systems and their approvals. Another common feature is AI because the prevailing state of drone technology shows a growing reliance on AI systems. It thus becomes imperative to read them in conjunction, as drone normalization is dependent on the regulatory approvals of such systems. Such political and legal analysis, as conducted in this article, shows a glaring inconsistency between the two visions. The inconsistency in different policies on the same point puts into question the institutional coherence within the EU, an idea that refers to a situation where 'a single policy area is served by two set of actors and their different procedures' (Marangoni & Raube, 2014, p. 475). As discussed in the succeeding section, drones form part of various European policy agendas, such as sustainability, green transition, security and defence, and urban mobility. Therefore, the alignment of visions around its integration ought to be well-tuned. A lack of consistency in such regard raises questions around political harmony amongst different institutions and their priorities, which may hinder different political agendas. This article begins by briefly introducing the two instruments through separate sections. In the subsequent section, I highlight the inconsistency between them by also touching upon the current state of drone technology. The concluding section then summarizes the findings and points to future implications of such inconsistency. The Drone Strategy 2.0 was released in November 2022 by the Directorate-General Mobility and Transport (DG MOVE), the DG in the EC with the political portfolio of mobility and transport, with the collaboration of different stakeholders. The instrument is also backed by a working staff document containing studies and surveys regarding drones. Despite its name, this strategy is the first of its kind, since it holistically covers various facets of civilian drone use such as civil-military synergies, counter drone technology, impact on sustainability, digitalization of European economy and aviation regulation. That comprehensiveness did not exist in the previous drone-related policies. In 2014, the EC came up with a similar instrument as the Drone Strategy 2.0, entitled 'A New Era for Aviation. Opening the Aviation Market to the Civil Use of Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems in Safe and Sustainable Manner' (EC, 2014). That communication highlighted the potential benefits of civilian drones and remarked a commitment towards rulemaking for its safety, security and privacy, as well as ensuring more investments in the research and development of this technology. It was followed by various instruments. Among them is the 2015 'Riga Drone Declaration' and Communication 'An Aviation Strategy for Europe' outlining aims for drone-related rules. In 2019, two regulations were passed covering the operations (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/947) and design (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/945) of civilian drones. In 2020, the EC passed the 'EU Security Union Strategy' and the 'Counter-Terrorism Agenda for the EU: Anticipate, Prevent, Protect, Respond', which touched upon the issue of counter drone technology. To deal with the issue of unmanned traffic management, also known as 'U-Space', the Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/664 (EC, 2021) was passed as the basis of U-Space. On the security and defence front, the 'Roadmap on Critical Technologies for Security and Defence' was passed in early 2022, holding relevance when it comes to dual-use technology research within the EU. One finds the explicit aim of formulating Drone Strategy 2.0 in the 2020 Communication for a 'Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy—Putting European Transport on Track for the Future', which generally outlined the future challenges and benefits offered by drones for European transport (EC, 2020). While the suffix '2.0' with Drone Strategy may give an impression that it is preceded by another similar holistic document, this is not the case, as highlighted above. Accordingly, the so-called 'Drone Strategy 1.0' is presumed to be a set of the referred action plans, communications, regulations and reports around civilian drones that have been produced up until the Drone Strategy 2.0 came about (EC, 2022b, p. 7); the most important of which I have mentioned in the previous paragraphs. Considering the nature and scope of this article, I have not addressed the full list of instruments that precede the strategy, but the ones covered here already provide a broad idea of the EC's endeavours around drone integration. A normalized drone ecosystem for EU citizens. EU citizens enjoying numerous drone services relating to emergency, inspections, surveillance and package delivery. Diverse use cases would emerge at an operational level and relevant EU institutions will have developed adequate capacity to ensure their safety and security. The unmanned traffic management system (which in the EU is named 'U-Space') will have the capacity to support large-scale and highly automated drone operations in several member states. Implicit in the above vision is the presumption that by 2030, the institutions, policies and standards would be sufficient to pave the way for drone normalization. However, the strategy suffers from obscurities by not addressing the regulatory efforts required for the integration of civilian drones (Scott & Andritsos, 2023) or considering the 'difficulty of scaling operations' (European Parliament, 2023, p. 11). Much could be questioned about the politics behind such high-level goals. For instance, less attention is paid to social acceptance (European Parliament, 2023, p. 69) or the issues of noise and visual pollution (Bergersen, 2021). However, this article is particularly interested in the planned standardization around AI systems and the regulatory approvals that will enable drone operations in civilian airspace. In such regard, the AI Roadmap released by the EU specialized aviation agency, EASA, holds great relevance. The next section analyzes that instrument. Level 1—Assistance to human. AI would augment (level 1A) or provide cognitive assistance (level 1B) to humans in the decision-making or execution process. Level 2—Human–AI teaming. AI would either cooperate (level 2A) or collaborate (level 2B) with humans. Level 3—Advanced automation. At level 3A, AI would decide and act while human would be able to override, whereas level 3B would be the highest level of automation where the AI system would not be overridable by a human. The envisioned timeline showing EASA's plan to develop necessary guidelines for each level and their consequent approvals is shown in Figure 1. In contrast to AI Roadmap 1.0, the second version extended years for approvals of commercial Single Pilot Operation from 2030 to 2035, and for autonomous AI (systems of the highest automation level) from 2035 to 2050+. This extension reflects EASA's realization of the complexities involved in developing standards and granting approvals for AI systems. Considering the later release of the AI Roadmap 2.0 than Drone Strategy 2.0, one expected more alignment in the visions and further clarity. Nonetheless, the modifications were crafted in a different fashion. The inconsistency arises because the systems that will normalize drone operations, as envisioned in the Drone Strategy, lie at level 3A. In addition, as can be seen in Figure 1, their approvals would not even commence before 2035. This section argues that such systems would lie at level 3A from two angles: first, by analysing EASA's elaboration of AI levels, and second, by highlighting the current state of drone technology. In early 2023, EASA proposed a concept paper for AI levels 1 and 2 (usable guidance for such applications) (EASA, 2023a). It explained that level 2 will allow human intervention in every decision-making and action. At level 3A, however, human intervention will be possible only where it is necessary for safety consideration. Interestingly, EASA exemplified level 3A as the one where a drone operator supervises a fleet of operations and is able to terminate the operation upon being alerted (EASA, 2023a, p. 27). As can be seen in Figure 1, level 3-related guidance is not even planned to emerge before 2028 and the first approvals would be granted from 2035. We also need to be mindful of the dynamic nature of this timeline as the roadmap 'will be revised, improved and enriched with time' as more experience is gained (EASA, 2023b, p. 5). Hence, it would be less surprising if EASA further extends the years for level 3 guidance and approvals in the upcoming roadmap. Moreover, EASA's approach is more gradual where heavy emphasis, for now, is laid on finalizing level 1 and 2 guidelines, and consequent approvals. This trend also eliminates the possibility of rapid action for level 3 before matters around levels 1 and 2 are fully finalized. The technological state of many prevailing drone operations renders them the status of AI level 3A because the remote pilot tends to be at the supervisory level (Scott & Nunes de Pinho Veloso, 2022, p. 14). Take as a practical example, the Wing delivery drones which are currently operating in Australia at a large scale. These operations allow pilot intervention in case the 'drones run outside a programmed flight' (Australian Civil Aviation Safety Authority, 2023). Hence, they fulfil the criteria of level 3A rather than level 2. Both the systems constituting the drone device and the traffic management system enabling large-scale drone operations in the EU (U-Space) will be highly automated.1 The U-Space will be backed by a number of mandatory services to ensure safe traffic, namely, flight authorization, traffic information, geo-awareness and network identification services. Currently, there is no regulatory clarity about the exact level of automation that will underpin these services. But if one considers the higher volume of drones one can imagine significantly lesser human involvement in U-Space than in the traditional manned air traffic. In view of the technological state of drone operations, EASA's envisioned pace fails to pave the way for the DG MOVE's vision of 2030. The normalization of drone ecosystem, numerous and diverse drone services, and large-scale traffic through U-Space are ambitious features of the Drone Strategy; they will require advanced levels of automation beyond mere assistance. On one hand, the EC sets a high-level goal of large-scale drone operations normalization in civilian airspace by 2030, while on the other hand, the specialized agency EASA does not even foresee the approvals for such operations before 2035. This is a glaring inconsistency between the political positions at the high and specialized levels within the EC. All that may potentially happen by 2030 is the normalization of level 1 AI systems (assistance to humans) where the control over systems would be with humans to a greater extent. As just discussed, civilian drone operations and the U-Space services that would manifest large-scale drone normalization would exceed level 1. The commitment to integrate drone technology in the civilian domain is quite prominent at the EU level. The Drone Strategy and EASA's AI Roadmap emerge as a reassurance of that commitment. However, in delineating the visions around it, the key European institutions lack coherence. Looking at the strategy, one gets an impression that EU airspace would be highly automated and digitalized by 2030, where drones would be operating with minimum human control. Yet, the EASA's roadmap extends quite the opposite impression for 2030. According to the latter, automation would be at a very low level, where humans would still be taking decisions and performing actions while the system would only be assisting them. Also, the current drone technology operates at a higher automation level. Complicating things further, the U-Space is also planned to be automated. Large-scale drone operations, as the strategy envisions, would thus not be possible at a low automation level. This article studied the most recent key policy instruments, but indeed with only two cases one cannot make out a case of general incoherence amongst EU bodies. Yet, the inconsistency exhibited in my analysis does raise questions about how coherent is policy-making at the general and specific levels within the EU. This case also highlights that the regulation and integration of new technologies is a mounting task, even for experienced regulatory entities such as the EU. This has important implications, because drones are increasingly penetrating in different European policy agendas, and therefore incoherent visions amongst institutions can cause political and regulatory challenges in the future. While harmonization between member states, the EC and the European Council in relation to the strategy remains a challenge (Lavallée & Martins, 2023), the inconsistency highlighted in this article raises questions about harmonization among EU bodies. These issues may also impact the global regulatory influence exercised by EU, a phenomenon labelled by Anu Bradford as the 'Brussels Effect', highlighting how EU policies in areas such as data protection, health and safety, and environment have become global standards (Bradford, 2020). These EU drone policies thus bear potential regulatory influence elsewhere too, and less attention paid towards noise or visual pollution, and on social acceptance of these measures, can create an undesirable precedent. Finally, for a political entity like the EU, issues of policy coherence also have crucial implications regarding the effectiveness, legitimacy and credibility of its actions (Marangoni & Raube, 2014, p. 486); for all these reasons, future regulatory efforts could benefit from greater consistency. RegulAIR: The integration of drones in the Norwegian and European Airspaces (2021–2024; Grant number: 314615) funded by the Research Council of Norway (RCN). Data sharing is not applicable to this article as no new data were created or analysed in this study.

title: Guest Editorial: Advances in Knowledge and Information Software Management
authors: Maria José Sousa; Pedro Henriques Abreu; Álvaro Rocha; Daniel Castro Silva
abstract: In today's global economy, Knowledge and Information Software Management is increasingly important in many organizations. Data are becoming larger, complex and more dynamic, creating a big challenge. Stimulating research in these areas has the goal of turning information overload into a significant opportunity and helping decision making in organizations. Information Software Management assumes a high importance and needs to be supported by highly interactive interfaces, tools and techniques in all aspects of computer science, engineering and business to synthesize information in order to manage and transform it into knowledge. Knowledge Management Software requires interdisciplinary science including knowledge representation, management and technologies. This Special Issue includes research papers that help develop and/or apply Knowledge and Information Software Management clearly, showing an interdisciplinary approach. The main issues discussed in this Special Issue are: a) Data management and knowledge representation; b) Knowledge engineering; c) Expert and knowledge-based systems; d) Information visualization software; e) Emergent technologies and software for knowledge management; f) Visual analytics software; g) Trends in Information and Knowledge Management. Most of the manuscripts are extended versions of selected papers from WorldCIST'16 – 4th World Conference on Information Systems and Technologies, held at Recife, Brazil, in 2016. The WorldCIST conferences have become an important forum for researchers and professionals to exchange ideas and experiences about research problems and corporate solutions related to information systems, technologies, and computer science in general. The eight selected articles in this Special Issue include a survey and case studies as well asworks that focus more on the design and implementation of knowledge management anddecision making tools. Borrego et al. (2017) present a systematic literature review of how Agile and Global Software Development companies handle Architecture Knowledge Management. They identify nine different approaches in the literature on how to deal with these two opposite paradigms, which the authors then group in three areas. Catal and Guldan (2017) use five classifiers with a majority voting combination rule to identify deceptive negative customer reviews. These fraudulent reviews are being used by companies to promote their own products and smirch their competition, and with customer reviews being a main factor for decision making, the detection and elimination of such fraudulent reviews is of paramount importance. In a healthcare domain, Nery et al. (2017) present a data mining approach to promote the early detection of leptospirosis cases, differentiating them from other illnesses with similar symptoms, and thus allowing for targeted treatments and a more auspicious outcome. Using the JRIP algorithm, the authors achieve good and promising results. Godinho et al. (2017) tackle the problem of Big Data in the medical imaging context. They presenta methodology for creating large medical imaging repositories based on existingsmaller datasets, by extracting data patterns and extrapolating a larger datasetthat meets the needs of any research study. Almonacid et al. (2017) present an approach to the Manufacturing Cell Design Problem using twometaheuristics: the Firefly Algorithm and the Egyptian Vulture OptimizationAlgorithm. The results are compared to those obtained using eight othermetaheuristics, and in some cases to the global optimum. Zhao et al. (2017) propose Colored Spatio-Temporal Petri Nets as an extension of colored Petri Nets to design and model Transportation Cyber-Physical Systems, thus better addressing the spatio-temporal discrete-continuous nature of these systems and the problems associated with it. They also present the Traffic Intersection Coordination Control System where they employ this methodology with promising results. Shan and Cao (2017) propose a methodology to leverage urban data and create an urban knowledge graph, which can then be used, together with a hybrid reasoning algorithm, to extract urban knowledge and reason over it. This can have multiple applications in the context of a smart city, helping with city planning and management. Jesus et al. (2017) present a study on the differences between learning styles in a therapeutics class. They compare face-to-face learning, traditionally used in this multidisciplinary course, and a blended learning approach, showing that there are differences between these two approaches. To conclude, we would like to thank all participants of WorldCIST 2016; in particular, we would like to thank the WorldCIST program committee members and the reviewers for this Special Issue of IET Software for their dedication and hard work. We hope this Special Issue will stimulate your interest in this area and spur you on to engage in further research in this field. As the Special Issue editors, we would like to take this opportunity to thank the various authors for their papers and the reviewers for their work. We are also grateful to Hana Chockler, IET Software Editor-in-Chief and the Editorial Office for their support throughout the editorial process. Maria José Sousa is a Professor at Universidade Europeia – Laureate International Universities, and at ISEG/IDEFE, Universidade de Lisboa. She is also a Post Doc researcher at University of Coimbra and received her Ph.D. degree in Management from Aveiro University. Her research interests are in the fields of Information Systems Management, Information Technologies in Education, Management and Innovation. In addition to her research expertise, she has extensive practical experience in public and private organizations. She is a researcher at Business Research Unit, Instituto Universitário de Lisboa, Portugal and at the CIEO – Research Centre for Spatial and Organizational Dynamics, University of Algarve. She is also an associate member of AISTI (Iberian Association for Information Systems and Technologies) and a member of the scientific committee of RISTI (Iberian Journal of Information Systems and Technologies). Pedro Henriques Abreu is an Assistant Professor at the Department of Informatics Engineering, University of Coimbra, Portugal. He obtained his Informatics Engineering Degree from the University of Porto in 2006 and a PhD in Soccer Teams Modelling also from the University of Porto in 2011. His interests include (but are not limited to) educational strategies, educational data mining, medical informatics and personal healthcare systems applied to oncological diseases. Pedro Henriques Abreu is the author of more than 50 publications in international conferences and journals. Álvaro Rocha holds Habilitation in Information Science, PhD in Information Systems and Technologies, MSc in Information Management, and Bachelor in Computer Science. He is Professor of Information Systems and Software Engineering at University of Coimbra, researcher at CISUC (Centre for Informatics and Systems of the University of Coimbra) and a collaborator researcher at LIACC (Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Computer Science) and at CINTESIS (Center for Research in Health Technologies and Information Systems). His main research interests are Information Systems Planning and Management, Information Systems Quality, Requirements Engineering, Software Engineering, e-Government, e-Health, and Information Technology in Education. He is President of AISTI (Iberian Association for Information Systems and Technologies), Chair of IEEE Portugal Section Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Society Chapter, and Vice-President of ADI-PME (Association for the Development and Innovation in the Small and Medium Enterprises). He is also the Editor-in-Chief of JISEM (Journal of Information Systems Engineering & Management) and the Editor-in-Chief of RISTI (Iberian Journal of Information Systems and Technologies). In addition, he is Vice-Chair of Experts in the Horizon 2020 of the European Commission, Expert in the COST - intergovernmental framework for European Cooperation in Science and Technology, Expert in the Italian Ministry of Education, University and Research, and General Chair of WorldCIST (World Conference on Information Systems and Technologies). He got his Informatics Engineering Degree from the University of Porto in 2006, and a PhD in Cooperative Multi- Vehicle Missions also from the University of Porto in 2011. His research interests include multi-agent systems, agent-based simulation, medical informatics and technology in education, among others. Daniel is the author of more than 50 publications in international conferences and journals.

title: Climate Constitutionalism of the UK Supreme Court
authors: Navraj Singh Ghaleigh
abstract: The proposed expansion of London’s Heathrow airport by way of a third runway is one-part infrastructure, two-part national soap opera. Legal controversy has been present from the first. The Heathrow site, previously orchard land, was acquired using emergency wartime powers in 1946, prompting decadal litigation.1 Plans for a third runway have a similar saga-like quality. Policy papers came and went, with the issue finally handed by Prime Minister David Cameron to a newly established Airports Commission in 2012.2 Guided by both the safe hands of Howard Davies (McKinsey, Bank of England, LSE, Man Booker Prize and so on), the Commission issued interim and final reports in 2013 and 2015, respectively, both recommending the north-west third runway option at Heathrow.3 After a parliamentary vote in 2018,4 it became the policy of the planning authority; that is, the Secretary of State for Transport, to approve the expansion, a decision which became the basis of the instant challenge. On 27 February 2020 the Court of Appeal of England and Wales handed down its judgment, on the challenge to the Secretary of State’s decision brought under the UK Planning Act 2008, section 13.5 Being one of the first appellate courts globally to be seised of a case requiring the consideration of Article 2 of the Paris Agreement (‘Agreement’), the decision appeared to give a steer as to how it could be deployed in domestic courts.6 Note that the UK government ratified the Paris Agreement on 17 November 2016, but that the treaty remains unincorporated. As such, obligations imposed on the UK Government by the Agreement eo ipso have no legal effect in domestic law.7 However, pursuant to section 5(8) of the Planning Act 2008 (‘Act’), policies such as those which purported to authorise the Heathrow extension, must give reasons for their decisions, including ‘an explanation of how the policy set out in the statement takes account of Government policy relating to the mitigation of, and adaptation to, climate change.’8 Two Ministerial Statements affirmed the Government’s commitment to enshrine the Paris goal of net-zero emissions in UK law.9 The question for the Court was whether the temperature target contained in Article 2 of the Agreement, or those ministerial statements, formed any part of relevant government policy within the meaning of the mentioned section 5(8). The Court of Appeal held that the Government erred by not taking the Paris Agreement and attendant policy explicitly into account. It was careful to make clear that the Secretary of State was not required to act in accordance with any particular policy, even the government’s own stated policy.10 However, an ordinary construction of the Act did require it ‘to take that policy into account and explain how it has been taken into account. None of that was ever done in the present case.’11 Moreover, the Court agreed with Plan B that the UK Government’s commitment to the Paris Agreement was clearly part of “Government policy” … this followed from the solemn act of the United Kingdom’s ratification of that international agreement in November 2016 [and] there were firm statements re-iterating Government policy of adherence to the Paris Agreement by relevant Ministers.12 The Court of Appeal’s conclusions had a mixed reception. It will be recalled that Prime Minister Boris Johnson was a long-standing opponent of the third runway, promising when Mayor of London to ‘lie down’ in front of bulldozers to stop the project.13 The Government decided not to appeal the Court of Appeal’s decision, but Heathrow Airport Ltd (‘HAL’), which owns Heathrow Airport did. The Supreme Court’s comprehensive reversal of the Court of Appeal was contained in a single, joint judgment of Lords Hodge and Sales. The personnel are somewhat noteworthy. There was a shiver of excitement amongst some in the climate community when in 2019 Lord Sales gave a lecture to the Anglo-Australasian Law Society entitled, ‘Directors’ duties and climate change: Keeping pace with environmental challenges.’14 The lecture ranged across materials known to many readers of JEL: the tragedy of the commons, stranding risks, the Task-Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, and their implications for company law and the various duties of directors. The argument, as might be expected, was exceptionally close and clear, and even trod lightly on the field of legislative reform. Sales were not the first Supreme Court Justice to opine extra-judicially on climate law—Lord Carnwath made a foray into this territory in 201515—but here was the intellectual star of the Supreme Court taking on a topic of some arcana, even for legal academia. To mangle Dr Johnson, the importance of the lecture for climate lawyers was not that it was well done (it certainly was), but that it was done at all. From this point, however, there were some missteps. There were conference conversations that Sales was ‘one of us’, that the tide of climate litigation was turning with a new generation of senior judiciary attuned to the climate crisis, that the Heathrow decision was in safe hands. Such views, which see law as a by-product of politics and policy without its own dynamics, have a long legal tradition. Horwitz termed them ‘Progressive Legal Thought’, to be contrasted with ‘Classical Legal Thought’.16 The latter, a species of formalism, is characterised by a mechanical application of legal rules without reference to external criteria or influences, the former is a more ‘realist’ attitude skeptical [sic] of strict divisions between legal and moral discourse. These models of public law adjudication have been exhaustively dissected, with their coexistence and shifting patterns being emphasised by scholars such as Duxbury, Stewart, Feldman.17 In UK studies of public interest litigation, including environmental, these arguments are best known from Harlow and Rawlings’ Pressure Through Law.18 Whatever one’s preferences as to judicial style—formalist or activist—instrumentalising judges as receptacles for particular ideologies is a risky business, not least since it strips law of its core characteristic, disinterested justice. And so it proved. The Supreme Court was straightforward in its departure from the Court of Appeal’s key findings. The style of the judgment is a powerful indicator of not just the outcome that the Court came to, but also its understanding of proper judicial method. Its first part is a close reading of the relevant statutory frameworks and their administrative operationalisation. The Act is parsed carefully, addressing in turn the mischief it addressed,19 its legislative development,20 and its substance of which National Policy Statements, integrating environmental, economic, and social objectives, is key.21 The Climate Change Act 2008 (‘CCA’) is initially set out more skeletally,22 and then analysed in the context of its application to the Heathrow planning decision,23 with the policymaking process of the implementation of the Paris Agreement recounted blow-by-blow. From ratification and National Determined Contribution (‘NDC’) submission, to ministerial statements, parliamentary debates, and numerous reports of the Climate Change Committee and Government responses, the judgment narrates an administrative system that is seriously engaged with its subject matter and working hand-in-glove with scientific expertise. Resembling a paean to the administrative state and its legislative frameworks, their Lordships’ decision was never in doubt. In the first ground, the ‘section 5(8) ground’,24 it was argued by Plan B that the government erred by treating as irrelevant the Agreement’s temperature target because section 5(8) of the Act required that the ANPS (the relevant national policy framework) explain how Government policy has been taken into account, and that the Agreement was government policy. The Court rejected the latter contention. Taking a purposive interpretation, the Court determined that ‘government policy’ was a term of art ‘to be given a relatively narrow meaning [such as] a formal written statement of established policy’.25 As such, the Ministerial Statements affirming the Government’s commitment to the Agreement were not ‘government policy’ within the meaning of the Act. That said, through the operation of the CCA however, the Agreement was well accounted for in Heathrow’s process. This was relevant for the second ground of review which related to section 10 of the Act, and its requirement that the Secretary of State acts with the aim of contributing to the achievement of sustainable development.26 As is well known, the CCA sets a national carbon target,27 requires Government to establish carbon budgets for the UK,28 and allows for adjustment of said targets and budgets29 as circumstances, including knowledge, change. Moreover, section 32 establishes the Committee on Climate Change, an independent and expert advisory public body. Understood in this framing, although the mechanisms of the CCA ‘masks somewhat the way the Paris Agreement did in fact enter into consideration by the Secretary of State’,30 the Secretary of State’s decision not to have further regard to the Paris Agreement beyond the CCA was not irrational.31 Furthermore, and at various points, the Supreme Court emphasised that future developments in climate science and policy would be considered at the Development Consent Order (‘DCO’) stage.32 The DCO is now the stage onto which the Heathrow drama moves. This is significant for both the framing of the litigation in terms of democratic principle, but also for the future of the project. The failure of the Plan B litigation to achieve its goal does not mean that the DCO process will move inexorably to the bulldozer stage, with all that that may entail for the physical integrity of the Prime Minister. Readers will recall the dismissal of Client Earth’s challenge to the Secretary of State’s decision to grant a DCO for the construction of new gas-fired units at the Drax Power Station.33 Nonetheless, weeks after their success in the Court of Appeal, Drax scrapped their plans for new gas owing to ‘the capital costs involved in building [which] would have been quite high and you’re really taking a long-term bet on where you think the power market is going to go.’34 The new economics of energy35 are succeeding in forcing fleet decarbonisation where law has failed. In a post-Covid world, who would bet against similar capital cost challenges for Heathrow? On a more principled level, the forum shift for the future determination of Heathrow’s fate keys into a familiar debate in constitutional law concerning the respective positions of political, expert and judicial determinations. Social democratic visions of public law have long been leery of judicial decision-making. Putting to one side the substance of social and economic objectives, they should be incorporated politically with courts being marginalised whilst democratically mandated public administrations and parliaments (in the Westminster model) pass laws, take decisions and scrutinise executives.36 This is commonly framed in terms of political constitutionalism (which privileges political forms and institutions of accountability) arrayed against legal constitutionalism (which privileges legal forms and institutions of accountability). In the current context, their Lordships took a view located squarely within the four corners of political constitutionalism and its conviction that ‘accountability is best secured through political institutions such as Parliament, by political actors such as parliamentarians and electors, and through political means such as debate, questioning, and investigative scrutiny.’37 This sits awkwardly with the current mania in academia and the campaigning community for ‘climate change litigation’38 which is routinely deeply embedded in legal constitutionalist thought, and its contention that ‘accountability is best secured through the legal institution of the courts, by judges, and through the legal means of adjudicative litigation.’39 Given the recently febrile relationship between UK courts and the executive (and indeed publics) ,40 principally surrounding Brexit, both the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court were at pains to make clear what they had and had not done. The Court of Appeal’s ruling was not, it said, a decision that there would be no third runway at Heathrow, nor that the policy statement supporting the project ‘was necessarily incompatible with the United Kingdom’s commitment to reducing carbon emissions and mitigating climate change under the Paris Agreement.’41 Rather, that Court concluded that Government may exercise the opportunity to reconsider its decision ‘in accordance with the clear statutory requirements that Parliament has imposed.’42 The Supreme Court’s decision sets yet more clear water between itself and the appearance of undue judicial intervention by declining to reduce the decision of Parliament and the Secretary of State, as determined by the Divisional Court. Rather than following the Court of Appeal it passed the matter on for decision to an expert limb of public administration (the Planning Inspectorate) established by statute (Planning Act 2008). No less importantly, the pained restraint of the Court may well be a harbinger of battles that climate litigation scholarship has yet to address. What if ‘we’ win? What if these actions succeed routinely and substantively? Legal scholarship has scarcely started to consider the impact of climate litigation on beneficiaries of pension funds that rely on the carbon majors, or considered the impact on workers in these defendant industries,43 though the union for aviation workers certainly had.44 In particular, further consideration is required of the risk of courtroom successes to the systems of law and courts by litigation which is funded by philanthropic foundations which are perceived as elitist, thereby risking populist counter-movements. The implications of ‘winning’ need analysis and planning, which whether as a policy or scholarly matter, has yet to begin in earnest. What does climate success look like? The dynamic review approach that the UK has taken to its climate targets, as advised by the Climate Change Committee and endorsed by this Supreme Court decision45 also has implications for future litigation. For example, the ‘Portuguese Children’s Case’ coordinated by the Global Legal Action Network, is currently in the pipeline of European Court of Human Rights. A full hearing is expected in the first half of 2022. A central claim in that action is that emission reduction targets less ambitious than 65% (1990 baseline) amount to an infringement of the applicants’ rights enshrined in Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention of Human Rights. Given the UK’s method of adjusting its emission reduction targets over time, on the basis of detailed multidisciplinary analysis and subject to public scrutiny, it will be interesting to see whether the Strasbourg Court does not determine that the detail of emission reductions—how much, in which sectors, by when and so on—are not within the province of Contracting States’ margin of appreciation. The Supreme Court’s decision on the proposed expansion of London’s Heathrow airport is in many ways a quintessential example of climate law. It engages multiple different bodies of law (international environmental, planning, administrative), the interface of climate science and industrial policy, and normative issues concerning the respective positions of political, expert and judicial determinations. Such clusters are characteristic of climate law, even inevitable. What is notable about this decision is its rejection of the attitude that there is no problem of climate law that cannot be solved by the courts, and that no climate law problem is truly solved until it is solved by a court.46 Viewed through that prism, the Plan B decision is a climate catastrophe, a legal abomination—and a galaxy of actors in the climate community wrote to say just that (though precious few domestic public lawyers among them).47 More plausible is the conclusion that the Supreme Court’s decision is soundly rooted in a constitutional theory of the court as supporting and nourishing the political constitution. As such this represents a timely recalibration of climate law discourse.

title: We need to chat about artificial intelligence
authors: Enrico W Coiera; Karin M. Verspoor; David P Hansen
abstract: With the arrival of large language models such as ChatGPT, AI is reshaping how we work and interact GPTs are a recent class of machine learning technology. Guided by humans who provide it with sample responses and feedback, ChatGPT was initially trained on 570 gigabytes of text, or about 385 million pages of Microsoft Word, and, at first release, the language model had 175 billion parameters.2 This massive model of the relationships between words is generative in that it produces new text, guided by the model, in response to prompts. It can answer questions, write songs, poems, essays, and software code. Other generative AIs such as DALL-E, which is trained on images, can create startlingly good pictures, including fictitious or "deep fake" images of real people.3 Today's LLMs are story tellers, not truth tellers. They model how language is used to talk about the world, but at present they do not have models of the world itself. The sheer size of ChatGPT means that it can perform tasks it was not explicitly trained to do, such as translate between languages. ChatGPT amassed 100 million users in the first two months that it was available.4 So compelling are the linguistic skills of LLMs that some have come to believe such AI is sentient,5 despite the prevailing view that as statistical pattern generators, they cannot have consciousness or agency. Australian singer Nick Cave called ChatGPT "a grotesque mockery of what it is to be human" after seeing it generate new songs in his style.6 The health care uses of generative models will soon become clearer.7 Epic has agreed with Microsoft to incorporate its GPT-4 model into their electronic health records, which have been used for over 305 million patients worldwide.8 LLMs are likely to find application in digital scribes, assisting clinicians to create health records by listening to conversations and creating summaries of the clinical content.9, 10 They can create conversational agents, which change the way we search medical records and the internet, synthesising answers to our questions rather than retrieving a list of documents.11 We should prepare for a deluge of articles evaluating LLMs on tasks once reserved for humans, either being surprised by how well the technology performs or showcasing obvious limits because of the lack of a deep model of the world.12 Especially when it comes to clinical applications, producing text or images that are convincing is not the same as producing material that is correct, safe, and grounded in scientific evidence. For example, conversational agents can produce incorrect or inappropriate information that could delay patients seeking care, trigger self-harm, or recommend inappropriate management.13 Generative AI may answer patients' questions even if not specifically designed to do so. Yet all such concerns about technology limitations are hostage to progress. It would be foolish indeed to see today's performance of AI as anything other than a marker on the way to ever more powerful AI. It is the unintended consequences of these technologies that we are truly unprepared for. It was hard to imagine in the early innocent days of social media, which brought us the Arab Spring,14 just how quickly it would be weaponised. Algorithmic manipulation has turned social media into a tool for propagating false information, enough to swing the results of elections, create a global antivaccination movement, and fashion echo chambers that increasingly polarise society and mute real discourse. Within two months of the release of ChatGPT, scientific journals were forced to issue policies on "non-human authors" and whether AI can be used to help write articles.15 Universities and schools have banned its use in classrooms and educators scramble for new ways to assess students, including returning to pen and paper in exams.16 ChatGPT is apparently performing surprisingly well on questions found in medical exams.17 The major unintended consequences of generative models are still to be revealed.18 LLMs can produce compelling misinformation and will no doubt be used by malicious actors to further their aims. Public health strategies already must deal with online misinformation; for example, countering antivaccination messaging. Maliciously created surges of online messages during floods, heat events, and pandemics could trigger panic, swamp health services, and encourage behaviours that disrupt the mechanics of society.19 With AI's many opportunities and risks, one would think the national gaze would be firmly fixed on it. However, Australia lags most developed nations in its engagement with AI in health care and has done so for many years.20 The policy space is embryonic, with focus mostly on limited safety regulation of AI embedded in clinical devices and avoidance of general purpose technologies such as ChatGPT. Some clinical colleges and organisations have been more "fleet of foot", adapting their training programs or developing frameworks for the ethical use of AI.21, 22 Yet there is currently no national framework for an AI-ready workforce, overall regulation of safety, industry development, or targeted research investment. The national conversation on AI in health care has for now remained niche and low in priority. Indeed, there has been a view in some quarters that all we need to do as a nation is adopt the best of what is produced internationally, and that we do not need deep sovereign capabilities. Nothing is further from the truth. Without some degree of algorithmic sovereignty (the capability to produce or modify AI in Australia), the nation is exposed to new risks and misses one of the most significant industrial revolutions of our times.23 We do not want to just export our clinical datasets and import back the models built with them. We should be a value adding economy that builds and exports these technologies ourselves. Australia's $1.4 billion clinical trials sector24 will face stiff international competition from those who use AI to identify, enrol and monitor patients more effectively and at a lower cost. Our health response to climate change will depend heavily on digital health and AI for mitigation and adaptation.25 Further, AI requires local customisation to support local practices and reflect diverse populations or health service differences.9 Without local capability, paying to modify clinical AI will likely become a huge burden on our health system. Critically, using AI requires retraining of the workforce, retooling health services, and transforming workflows. The health system is already resource-constrained, and such changes will not happen without strategic investment. The national discussion on what to do next has begun, with a roadmap for AI in health care produced by the Australian Alliance for AI in Healthcare (AAAiH) — a national collective of over 100 organisations including academia, industry, peak bodies, and health services providers.26 The roadmap is the product of feedback from 152 key stakeholder organisations and individuals and contains 24 recommendations across eight priority areas. The highest community priority identified was for health care AI to be safe for patients and developed and used ethically. AI privacy and data security were another major concern. Respondents identified the need for genuine whole-of-nation leadership in the health care AI space as well as robust governance of the sector. Gaps in our workforce capability to build and use health care AI were clearly identified, as was the need for consumers to be fully engaged in shaping the health care AI agenda. Respondents also rated the gaps in our capability to adopt AI into practice and the need to enhance local industry capability as issues needing clear attention. While a great start, the roadmap now needs to be converted into action, and that will require bringing together the skills and interests of many stakeholders, from government, consumer bodies, clinicians, industry, health service providers, and academia. We can only expect the pace of AI innovation to accelerate, and for its consequences, good and ill, to multiply. We have a national imperative to both harness and benefit from these technologies, and not be hostages to the decisions of others. The time for urgent national engagement has arrived. Enrico Coiera is also supported by an NHMRC Investigator Grant (GNT2008645). The funders had no role in this manuscript. This article was written without the assistance of ChatGPT or other large language models.
